SOUTHERN MANITOBA
subsubtopic: BENEFIT BARN DANCE FOR RELIEF FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I rise on a point of personal privilege. Following a lengthy telephone conversation last night with a group of my constituents, I wish to announce that a huge benefit bam dance will be held at my farm early in June, and that the total proceeds will be turned over to the Manitoba flood relief fund.
My point of privilege is this. We are flood-conscious, and wish to stress the need to help those people who were so unfortunate as to be forced from their homes by this disastrous flood.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxfon (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
maintopic: EXCHANGE OF TELEGRAMS BETWEEN PRIME MINISTERS OF THE UNITED KINGDOM AND CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the following telegram has been received from the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom
through the Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations, addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs:
On behalf of my colleagues and myself I should like to convey to you the deep concern with which we have learned of the serious floods in Winnipeg. Please express our heartfelt sympathy with those who have suffered in the catastrophe.
The following telegram was sent by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to Mr. Attlee:
My colleagues and I deeply appreciate the United Kingdom government's message of sympathy for those who are suffering from the serious floods in Manitoba. Your message reached me just before I went into the House of Commons today and I made it public from my place in the house.
Subsequent to those messages we received from the Secretary of State for External Affairs and our high commissioner on the other side the report of an interview with Mr. Attlee, at which Mr. Attlee asked if there was any way in which the help of the United Kingdom government or its people could be extended to the people of Manitoba. That offer was very warmly received and has been communicated to the premier of Manitoba.
Mr. . George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):	Mr. Speaker, I should like to
associate myself with the statement made by the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Claxton) as to the appreciation which I am sure is felt by every member here as a representative of his constituency, of the generous and sympathetic offer made by the government of the United Kingdom. Undoubtedly the way in which this offer was made will help to continue and to emphasize the warm and friendly association which exists, and I hope will always exist, between this country and the United Kingdom.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF POSTPONEMENT OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
ANNOUNCEMENT OF POSTPONEMENT OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for the information of hon. members and the interested public I feel I should announce that the dominion-provincial conference on rehabilitation of the handicapped, which was scheduled to be held in Ottawa May 25 to 27, has been postponed on account of the Manitoba flood. Upon the suggestion of the premier of Saskatchewan, and after consultation with the health authorities of Manitoba and Alberta, this action was found advisable. Many of the delegates from these three provinces who would like to attend the conference, are busily engaged in looking after sufferers and evacuees from the flood area. The interdepartmental committee, made up of representatives of the departments of labour, health and welfare, and veterans affairs studied the situation at a special meeting, but were unable to suggest another suitable time for the conference because of the difficulty of getting accommodation. However, it should be clearly understood that the conference will be held as soon as circumstances permit.

speechtext: On the order for motions:

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
subtopic: SUMMARY OF DECISIONS TAKEN BY THE COUNCIL IN LONDON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members will be aware, the North Atlantic council, which has been meeting in London since May 15, completed its sessions

yesterday. The following is the text of the communique issued by the council summing up the decisions taken in London:
The North Atlantic council established in accordance with article 9 of the treaty has so far only met twice at the ministerial level and on two other occasions when members of the council have been represented by their governments' diplomatic representatives in Washington.
But under article 9 the council is the principal body of the North Atlantic treaty. It is therefore the paramount duty of the council to put itself in a position to exercise its full role as the central and most important of the various organs of the treaty by taking the most effective steps to keep itself informed of all matters which fall within its competence, by taking the necessary decisions and by ensuring the execution of such decisions.
A year's experience has shown that on the political side the meetings of the council have been too infrequent to permit a sufficient exchange of views on matters of common interest within the scope of the treaty. On the military side the strategic concept of the treaty has been adopted and a defence plan drawn up and the corresponding estimate of the necessary forces is being established. The next step is to put these plans into effect by taking further measures in the direction of common defence, the division of financial responsibilities and the adaptation and development of the necessary forces.
In view of this situation, the council will in particular undertake the following task:
(a)	Study the interrelationship of the various programs to support the plans for the defence of the north Atlantic area and ensure co-ordination of the work of the defence committee, the defence financial and economic committee, and all other bodies established under the North Atlantic treaty organization.
(b)	recommend to governments the steps necessary to ensure that effect is given to the co-ordinated plans prepared for the defence of the north Atlantic area.
(c)	Exchange views on political matters of common interest within the scope of the treaty.
(d)	Promote and co-ordinate public information in furtherance of the objectives of the treaty while leaving responsibility for national programs to each country.
(e)	Consider what further action should be taken under article 2 of the treaty, taking into account the work of existing agencies in this field.
To enable the council effectively to carry out its responsibilities and to exercise them continuously, each government will appoint a deputy to its council representative. Each deputy will be in a position to give whatever time may be necessary to ensure that the responsibilities of the council are carried out effectively.
In the intervals between meetings of ministers, the deputies, duly authorized by their respective governments, will be responsible, on behalf of and in the name of the council, for carrying out its policies and for formulating issues requiring decisions by the member governments.
The council, having considered the reports of the defence committee and the defence financial and economic committee, issued directives to guide them in their future work. These directives emphasize that the problem of adequate military forces and the necessary financial costs should be examined as one and not as separate problems.
In formulating their directives the council proceeded on the basis that the combined resources of the members of the North Atlantic treaty are sufficient, if properly co-ordinated and applied, to

ensure the progressive and speedy development of adequate military defence without impairing the social and economic progress of these countries.
The council, recognizing the indispensability of self-help and mutual aid among the treaty powers in making progress towards an integrated defence, and convinced that further mutual assistance is essential to rapid progress towards the strength required for the common security of the north Atlantic area, recommended that each party make its full contribution through mutual assistance in all practicable forms.
The council unanimously agreed that if adequate military defence of the member countries is to be achieved it must be along the lines of the most economical and effective utilization of the forces and material at the disposal of the north Atlantic countries. They accordingly urged their governments to concentrate on the creation of balanced collective forces in the progressive build-up of the defence of the north Atlantic area, taking at the same time fully into consideration the requirements for national forces which arise out of commitments external to the north Atlantic area.
In furtherance of article 9 of the treaty the council established a North Atlantic planning board for ocean shipping, to be composed of representatives of the participating countries concerned. This board will report directly to the council and will work in close co-operation with other bodies of the treaty organization in all matters relating to the factor of merchant shipping in defence planning.
The ministers believe that the decisions they have taken here in London represent a marked advance towards the practical realization of the objectives of the North Atlantic treaty.
It is evident that this has been the most important meeting of the North Atlantic council so far. Decisions have been taken which should ensure that the gathering strength of the North Atlantic treaty nations is organized in the most efficient fashion for the defensive purposes of the treaty and that progress will be made in the fields of political and economic co-operation. We have taken a long step forward, and I know that hon. members will fully realize the importance of these developments in building up a stable and prosperous north Atlantic community.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: SUMMARY OF DECISIONS TAKEN BY THE COUNCIL IN LONDON
speechtext:
The announcement which we have just heard, Mr. Speaker, and which we read earlier in the press, as to the unanimous decision of the representatives of the twelve nations of the Atlantic community is an announcement of what is undoubtedly the most momentous decision that has been made since the summer of 1945. Until this decision was reached yesterday, the Atlantic treaty and the set-up of the council still left some uncertainties as to the full scope of their activities. Even yesterday in his announcement of the earlier report the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) emphasized the fact that the discussions had been informal. The announcement which has now been made carries this matter far beyond the stage of informality. 1 feel sure that hon. members will welcome the fact that this matter has passed the stage of informal discussion 55946-168
North Atlantic Treaty and that now there is in definite form a permanent executive committee of the Atlantic council to which there will be a Canadian delegate with appropriate secretarial and official assistants.
It cannot be emphasized too often that at this very time we are passing through the most critical stage of modern history. I feel sure that the hon. members of this house of all parties will wish that the Canadian representative on that committee, whoever he may be, will at all times act with the knowledge that in the joint efforts to preserve peace there is complete unanimity in this house.
While that meeting does not deal with anything except the organization of the nations of the Atlantic community, it has been noticeable that in the reports of those discussions, which by more than coincidence take place at the same time as the conference in Sydney, there has been reference to the problems of the Pacific. I do not think it would be appropriate to allow an occasion of this kind to pass without bringing forward the suggestion that the free nations of the world will not have completed their task of containing and restraining communist aggression until they have taken similarly effective steps amongst the free nations of the Pacific community.
This is a great step forward; but at the moment the most vigorous communist pressure is in southeast Asia. Those who live in the free nations of that area are emphasizing the need for recognition of immediate action. I would express the earnest hope that, with this very real achievement to the credit of the Atlantic community, steps will be taken without delay to bring similar results in that complementary area where communism is so active today.
All security depends upon security from aggression. The Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Claxton) has pointed out that this permanent body which will be set up will deal not only with the military but also with the financial questions as one problem. To a great extent it might be said at the same time that the problem of advancing the social security and general welfare of the people in these and other free nations is directly related also to military and economic concerns.
There is one point of great importance mentioned by the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs which raises another consideration which I think should be brought forward immediately. The decisions yesterday have created a new North Atlantic planning board for ocean shipping, composed of representatives of the maritime nations within

North Atlantic Treaty this group of Atlantic nations. It is to be the purpose of that permanent planning board to plan for the preparation of adequate shipping and for the mobilization of that shipping in the event of an emergency. This, I say, immediately raises a consideration of great importance to every Canadian. In view of the fact that Canada has now agreed to become a part of a permanent planning board for maritime shipping in relation to the general world problem, I hope that it will mean the immediate re-establishment of the Canadian flag fleet.

speechtext:
As
I listened to the statement read by the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Claxton) a line or two of Tennyson came to my mind, namely:
The old order changeth, yielding place to new.
As I listened today and last evening to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) I
[Mr. Drew.l
thought of the extent to which the old order was giving way to the new; that a few years ago we thought it impossible that the nations of the Atlantic community, for example, could co-operate economically, socially and in our common defence. The statement made today and last night has impressed upon this house, as it must have impressed the countries of the Atlantic community, the fact that in all our domestic policies, whether they be economic or social, we have to consider their impact upon the rest of the members of that community. I said last night that I thought that perhaps more important than the military arrangements made among the ministers in London during the past few days were the arrangements for economic and social co-operation.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) mentioned southeast Asia. I firmly believe that there can be no defence against communism, or any other form of totalitarianism, in southeast Asia unless the nations of the world co-operate to improve the standards of living of the people of that part of the world. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we welcome this statement, and I can assure the government, the leader of the opposition and the members of the house that anything we can do to advance this great idea of co-operation first among the members of the Atlantic community, and then among the members, we hope, of the great world community, we shall be pleased to support and indeed to undertake.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROCUREMENT OF MILITARY EQUIPMENT BY UNITED STATES IN CANADA

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROCUREMENT OF MILITARY EQUIPMENT BY UNITED STATES IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have one further announcement of very great importance to make; but before doing so may I say how much the government appreciates the expressions of support and unity on the part of the leaders of the various parties who have spoken. It indicates that so far as defence and external policy are concerned, Canada is united to a greater extent than ever before.

Hon. members wui nave seen press reports regarding the procurement by the United States of military equipment in Canada.
I am glad to be able to inform the house that it has been announced officially in Washington that the United States service departments and munitions board have been requested by the Secretary of Defence to develop a program for the purchase in Canada, during the year beginning next July 1, on a reciprocal basis, of military equipment to the value of between fifteen and twenty-five million dollars.
This announcement marks a major step in the integration of military production in the two countries. It is an extension into the peacetime period of the principles of the Hyde Park declaration of 1941, which proved so effective during wartime.
This announcement comes as a result of negotiations which I initiated with the late James Forrestal but which were carried through by Hon. Louis Johnson, Secretary of Defence, following a recommendation by the permanent joint board on defence. It is something for which we have all been working for some time.
It is still too early to indicate what this may mean in terms of specific items, but I can say with assurance that the benefits that may be realized under this arrangement will contribute not only to the defence potential of both countries and consequently the defence of our continent, but also to the over-all defence arrangements under the North Atlantic treaty.

The bill therefore is before the house now in the same form as that which I had in mind when it was first discussed in the resolution stage. But after listening to the discussion, and for some other reasons, I have concluded that it would be best to send this bill to the committee on agriculture and have it discussed there. I have had a wire from the minister concerned in Alberta, namely, the minister of municipal affairs and provincial secretary. I believe he might desire to appear before the committee, and I have wired him saying that it would be quite proper for him to do so if he so desires. I have also had a letter from the minister of agriculture in Saskatchewan setting forth some points of view in the matter.
I think it would be helpful to have the measure come before the committee, and have any amendments we desire to make to the bill as it was submitted, in printed form, proposed when it is before the committee.
I wish to refer only in a general way to the amendments we had already decided to introduce in certain forms which may or may not be entirely satisfactory to the committee.
The legislation as it now stands indicates that it is the desire of the government to avoid the payment of prairie farm assistance on lands which, over a long period of time, were open for homesteading, and were not considered of sufficient fertility or good enough to be taken up as homesteads; or if they were, by action of the federal government while the resources were under its control, such action
Prairie Farm Assistance Act being continued by the provincial governments after the lands were taken over by them, withheld from settlement under the homesteading plan, such lands should not now be permitted to come in under prairie farm assistance legislation. It would appear that the terms of the present act could be a consideration when taking up lands under the provisions which are set out in some of the provincial legislation. That legislation does make it possible for persons to go on some of those lands on cultivation leases.
I think it is most important that it be clearly demonstrated to all parties concerned that any lands which are going to be opened up for cultivation now are lands upon which there is some opportunity for persons who settle on them to make a living, without any assistance, from this government in particular. Whether the bill went to the committee or not we had expected to bring in amendments to make our view definite.
When I was speaking the other night I said that there was no doubt that lands which were under co-operatives as understood in Saskatchewan would not be excluded merely by the fact that they operated as co-operatives and the lands were still owned by the government. However, on. rereading the act I find that when we were amending it before we took a short cut. Instead of definitely saying that that was the case, we amended the definition of "farmer" in order to have it cover a man who was on a co-operative farm and who would therefore be entitled to payment. When we definitely eliminated the land I think probably we eliminated the individual. The proposal was definitely to put into the section being amended a provision that those who are on co-operative farms in the sense I have just spoken of shall not be eliminated by this section.
Then it was hoped that we could devise some amendment to deal with the situation which has been created in connection with several areas in Alberta and which would be satisfactory to those who are settled in those areas and to the government here. Even if the bill had not gone to the committee it was proposed to introduce an amendment to make it clear that certain persons living in those special areas would not be debarred from receiving prairie farm assistance.
All I intend to do at this stage is to move the second reading of the bill in order to get it to the committee as soon as possible, and also to make it known to the governments and others who may be concerned that it will be possible for them to place their cases before the committee and have the matter considered at as early a date as possible. If that meets

Prairie Farm Assistance Act with the approval of the house, I would suggest that we might satisfy ourselves with giving the bill second reading and permit it to go to the committee where the whole matter could be fully discussed. The bill could then be brought back to the house, where a full discussion could take place, and when hon. members would be in possession of information on which to base a decision.
Since we were dealing with this legislation the other evening I have experienced great difficulty in getting up-to-date copies of the different provincial acts. We have wired for many of these and have received some, but not all. I think it would be well if we had all the legislation before the committee when we were discussing this matter.
I may say that one of the matters I was concerned with, and with which the government was concerned, is the fact that there has been a much greater growth recently in the payments than perhaps anyone expected. Apart altogether from the fact that we have not increased the amount per acre, there has been a considerable increase in the total amount which has been paid. Last year the payments exceeded $20 million. I would hope that we could put this legislation on such a basis that it will not eventually be criticized because the payments are out of proportion to what ought to be paid or because payments are being made on land on which we should not make payments.
In the communications I have had from the provincial governments they have expressed views along similar lines, namely, that it is their intention not to insist upon lands being taken in, but rather to try to get a decision which will be satisfactory to all without bringing in land which should not be included.
If the house is prepared to give the bill second reading, I shall then move that it be referred to the committee on agriculture, to be fully considered and returned to the house later.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there will be full agreement by the members of this party with the suggestion that the bill be referred to the committee on agriculture. However, there are other phases of the matter which I suggest should be submitted to the committee. I can understand as suggested by the minister that with the rapidly accelerating amounts that are being paid out under this most beneficial legislation, the time may come when criticisms will seriously impair its operation.
As I understand it, the reason for the legislation was and is to keep farmers on lands where, as a result of drought and other causes, there may be crop failures. Everyone makes his contribution of one per cent, and

everyone making that contribution within the limitations set by the legislation receives payment. That is the understanding and conception of the farmers with regard to this legislation-at least of those in my constituency and in other parts of Saskatchewan with whom I have spoken.
But legislation passed by parliament is subject to regulations which may be passed under the powers contained in the act, and in this instance, as I see it, many are being denied prairie farm assistance because of the regulations. The regulations have been amended from time to time to define the meaning of owner or tenant. "Farmer" means a person who is the owner or tenant and who operates a farm in the spring wheat area, or who as a member of a co-operative farm association is engaged in farming in the spring wheat area. That was the definition that parliament gave to "farmer".
I agree with the minister when he says that if land is to be removed from the operation of the act in the manner indicated by him, then the law as it now stands would deny payments under the act to co-operatives holding land in the areas referred to by him. In 1949 serious crop failures, covering a large area, occurred in Saskatchewan, and yet many farmers were denied prairie farm assistance who, as I see it, ought to have received it. They are denied that assistance in part by reason of the limitations created by the definition of owner or tenant in the regulations. Under the regulations owner or tenant is defined as follows:
An owner or tenant is not a farmer for the purposes of this act:
(a)	unless he is the owner or tenant of a farm from the first day of May to the first day of November in the same year;
(b)	unless he lives in the spring wheat area and his primary occupation is farming from the first day of May to the conclusion of the crop season;
(c)	unless he is responsible for the farm operations and the disposal of the proceeds of the farm; and
(d)	if renting from a parent, unless he has a written lease executed prior to the first day of May of the year of award.
I am not going to concern myself with paragraphs (a) and (d). When they were first introduced, paragraph (d) in particular, they did have the result of denying many people their undoubted right to the payment of this bonus, for many were unaware of the existence of these regulations during the year they were brought in. I take objection to paragraph (b), however, which provides that an owner or tenant is not a farmer for the purposes of this act unless he lives in the spring wheat area and his primary occupation is farming from May 1 to the end of the crop season.

Many people are being denied the bonus under that paragraph. Many farmers in the drought areas of Saskatchewan-and I speak particularly of those areas though my argument applies as well in Manitoba and Alberta -know by June 15 or thereabouts whether there are any prospects of a crop that year. Many of them, finding themselves in the position of having to support wives and families, have to leave their farms at that time and accept work elsewhere.

speechtext: If I might interrupt for a moment, I think my hon. friend is suggesting that this provision is contained only in the regulations. It is in the act as well.

speechtext:
I realize that, but it is being interpreted in a way that parliament never intended. I could give example after example; and the regulations are not applied uniformly. Some farmers get the bonus though they have left their land because of the conditions with which they are faced, while others in the same position are denied it. There is no uniformity in the application of that section. Too many are being denied payment of the bonus, when fully qualified for it, by a too strict interpretation on the part of those administering the act. I feel that paragraph (b) should be administered in a generous manner. I am not arguing for the person who has a full-time occupation other than farming, who is in business and operates a farm as well. I am arguing for the right of the individual who operates a business as a side line, if you will, or takes work as a side line because of the fact that early in the year he is almost assured of a crop failure.
Many have been denied the bonus. The records reveal a situation that is challenging. The minister mentioned the fear that if the amount expended in this way continues to increase, objection will be raised to the continuation of this legislation. Indeed, reading between the lines of the speech he made a week ago today there would seem to be clear evidence that objection is now being raised in certain quarters to the continuance of this legislation in its present form. I placed a question on the order paper asking how many farmers in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba who had applied for payment of the bonus had been denied it, and that question was answered in a return on May 8. These are farmers who suffered failure and, in consequence of such crop failure last year, are having difficulty in financing their operations this year. The number who have been denied payment under the act is extraordinarily large. Because this record does not appear in Hansard I intend to read it; for it reveals
Prairie Farm Assistance Act a situation serious in its import and effect. Perhaps if the house would consent I could place this return on Hansard, and then I would not need to read it in detail.

The return states:
Question:
1.	How many (a) individual (b) township applications, for payment of P.F.A. were refused or denied in each of the prairie provinces between the first day of July, 1949, and the first day of February, 1950?
2.	(a) How many cases, in each province, was the refusal or denial of payment under the PF.A.A. submitted to the board of review? (b) What is the total number of cases in each province in which the said board reversed the decision appealed from?
The attached information has been received by the Secretary of State of Canada from the Department of Agriculture.
Answer of Department of Agriculture
1.	(a) Saskatchewan-1320; Manitoba-84; Alberta -249.
(b) Applications are made by the municipalities, and the provinces for unorganized areas, who give an estimate only of the average yield of wheat in the township applied for. No records are kept of ineligible townships except those that are contiguous to eligible areas, this being for the purpose of determining eligible blocks of sections therein.
2.	(a) Saskatchewan-136; Manitoba-3; Alberta- 19.
(b) Saskatchewan-19; Manitoba-nil; Alberta-3.
That return indicates that in 1949 some 1,320 farmers in Saskatchewan were refused payment of the bonus between July 1, 1949, and February 1, 1950. In Manitoba the number was 84, and in Alberta 249. Some of these applications were submitted to the board of review. In Saskatchewan only 19 of the total number of appeals were allowed. In Manitoba only three appealed and no appeal was allowed, while in Alberta out of 19 appeals three were allowed.
What do the figures for Saskatchewan indicate? Taking the average farm at 320 acres, which I think is a fair rule of thumb for Saskatchewan, it means that last year farmers of some 425,000 acres, who suffered drought and crop failure and felt qualified to obtain payment under this legislation, were in fact denied payment. It reveals that in the *operation of this act, and in part at least particularly in its administration, the rules are too strictly interpreted. I have examples of farmers living side by side. One got the payment; the other, across the road, was denied it under identical circumstances, though both were within a qualified area, because of interpretations placed by the commission upon the meaning of "owner" or "occupant" under the definition I have read.
2658	HOUSE OF
Prairie Farm Assistance Act I feel it only fair in the exercise and discharge of its responsibilities and in the interpretation of these regulations that the board of review should act not in a restrictive manner but in a manner that will bring about to the greatest possible extent fairness, equality and uniformity in the operation of this act.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, farmers occupying at least 425,000 acres of land in the province of Saskatchewan, who believe themselves qualified for this bonus, were denied it last year. This reveals a serious situation, which demands the attention of this house. When the committee commences to sit on this matter, I should like the whole question of the regulations to be submitted to it, to the end that the opinions of the farmer members on the committee could be secured, and if necessary the opinions of those outside the house who believe that changes should be made in connection with the administration of this legislation.
I come now to a phase to which reference was made by the minister, and it is one that raises a great deal of difficulty. It is the fact that over the years in parts of the western provinces, for a period indeed of nine and ten years, bonus payments have been made in the same areas. It indicates that there are certain areas wherein the probability of crops being harvested is extremely remote. I am not going into the figures for the areas in which payments have been made over a successive period of three, four or five years but will restrict my argument to the areas, by townships, in which payments have been made from seven to ten times since 1939. Under this heading in the province of Saskatchewan 329 townships have received payments for seven years since 1939;	294 townships have
received payments for eight years in the same period; 162 townships have received payments for nine years in that period, and finally in 44 townships there have been bonus payments for ten years since 1939. Those are striking figures and they warrant the admonition that was given by the minister in his opening remarks.
In parts of the province of Alberta the situation is fairly serious. Payment has been made for seven years out of the period of eleven years since 1939 in 71 townships; for eight years in 121 townships; for nine years in 177 townships, and for ten years since 1939 the bonus has been paid in 41 townships. From those figures one must realize that something must be done. It is because those areas have been so continuously denied a crop that we in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta are demanding that ' action be taken to provide irrigation by


proceeding with the work as soon as possible on such projects as the south Saskatchewan river irrigation scheme. Those areas would be productive were it not for the lack of moisture. They could be made productive. After listening to the revelations made by the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Claxton), wherein he stated that Canada intends, with the nations of the Atlantic community, to co-ordinate our economic development, I believe that one course Canada must take in order to meet the situation in southeast Asia, referred to by the leader of the opposition, is to expand our agricultural production and give assistance to the people in southeast Asia, and particularly in India, Pakistan and Ceylon. This would enable those areas, under the development of the plans of the North Atlantic pact, or if necessary a Pacific pact, to provide for the containment of communism where it now is. It would deny the extension of communism by reason of hunger into India, Pakistan, Ceylon and the other countries of that area.
We in this country have a responsibility in connection with our agricultural production that challenges the Minister of Agriculture, and all those charged with the extension and expansion of agricultural production, if we are to meet the commitments we accepted in London yesterday as a member of the community of north Atlantic countries.
Returning once more to the amendments that are before the house, I communicated with many rural municipalities in the area particularly subject to drought, with a view to securing from the municipalities their recommendations as to changes in the law that might be made. Some of their suggestions have been made previously in this house. Some of them were made two years ago when I spoke on this matter, and some are the result of recent experience. It seems that many of them have gone further than ever before in suggesting that, in order to maintain the prairie farm assistance payments, realizing the difficulties of establishing crop insurance, it might well be necessary to make some increase in the amount of contribution. The minister mentioned that in recent years there has been a considerable acceleration in the expenditure in this connection. An answer given on March 16 to the member for Souris (Mr. Ross) reveals that since the inception of this act the total contributions made amount to $45,008,887. The total amount expended during the same period has been $123,876,630; that amount may have increased somewhat since this return was brought in some two months ago.

speechtext:
The return, then, is
approximately correct. It indicates that a vast area in the western provinces has suffered from the destruction of crops last year as a result of drought, grasshoppers and the like. The area in Manitoba was 82 townships; in Alberta, 1,126 townships; and in Saskatchewan, 1,731 townships. These figures underline the necessity for something being done in order to improve productivity, by the assurance of moisture through irrigation in a large portion of the areas comprised within these townships.
A general summary of the recommendations made by the rural municipalities, and I communicated with seventy rural municipalities so that I would have a cross-section of their suggestions and recommendations, is as follows:	(1) somewhat different from
the attitude some years ago when many advocated an individual basis as the basis upon which payments should be made, the general suggestion now seems to be that the area itself, in certain portions of Saskatchewan, should be reduced to the half township area. I refer to those areas adjacent to the Qu'Appelle valley where veterans were settled after the first war. They were settled along the eastern side of the Qu'Appelle valley. Over the years these people have lived in hope but have suffered repeated failures and because of the fact that part of the townships in which they farm is situated on the west side of the valley, they have been denied payment over the years. There are about nine areas in Saskatchewan in that position. I feel that something should be done in this committee to recommend some change in the law to meet this localized situation. I do not like to ask for laws applicable to particular areas, but there are in Saskatchewan seven or nine areas that are in this position. The people want to live there. They do not want to leave. They believe they should be entitled to consideration on the part of parliament to the extent of their areas being made subject to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and qualified either under regulation or under amendment to the act.
The second is this: while every farmer who suffers failure within the qualified areas should be entitled to the payment of a bonus,
provided his primary occupation is farming, nonetheless, in the definition of what "primary occupation" is, too many are being denied payment. Several of these municipalities have pointed out examples in their area where farmers who found it necessary to leave the farm temporarily because they were 55946-169
Prairie Farm Assistance Act facing failure, and realized they were facing failure that year, have been denied payment. These municipal officers say that in the interpretation of "primary occupation" there is too strict an adherence to the letter of the law rather than to the spirit of it.
The third recommendation that is comprised in many of the suggestions is a request in connection with the amounts that are payable for crop failure bonus which were fixed on the basis of conditions in 1939, namely, $2.50 or $1.50 an acre, depending on the degree of failure. Having regard to the taxation that they pay these municipalities say that there is no reason whatsoever why there should not be an increase in the amount of assistance payable. The amount of P.F.A. that is payable today is insufficient to place a farmer in a position in which he can continue his farming operations; and after all, that was the purpose for which this legislation was passed.
I do not want to go into further detail. I believe, however, that these suggestions are worthy of consideration by the committee on agriculture that is to inquire into the matter of amendments to the law as it now stands. The bringing into effect of a few of these suggestions that I have placed before you, Mr. Speaker, would go far towards removing a feeling sometimes approaching resentment that one finds where farmers are denied payment because of the interpretation placed on the regulations or because of the narrowness of the qualification as provided by law.
The changes I recommend, if accepted, would have the result of removing almost every objection that is to be heard with regard to this legislation. It has worked out well. It is a monumental example of the nation's desire to accept responsibility for the failures of fellow Canadians who suffer failure by reason of circumstances beyond their control.
We in the province of Saskatchewan have received much more than we have ever paid. We recognize and appreciate that fact. In Saskatchewan, the contribution over the years under this legislation has been some $24,600,000. The amount paid to Saskatchewan farmers has amounted to some $95 million. We recognize that fact, and we appreciate what other parts of the country have done to show that, where what amounts to a national disaster happens to agriculture in the western provinces, the people of Canada as a whole are willing to help us in our difficulties.
In that spirit, realizing what has been done for us, we in Saskatchewan-and I impress this upon the government, though I speak as a member of the opposition-will

Prairie Farm Assistance Act join with them in anything they may do to assist the people of Winnipeg and the peoole of Manitoba in general in the disaster that has come to that province in recent weeks. We believe- it is a national disaster. We believe that the people of Manitoba ought to be assured that Canadians as a whole will do everything they can to reimburse them financially, so that their losses will be borne as far as possible by the nation at large. After all, national disasters demand national consideration, and are no longer matters of provincial responsibility alone.

I regret, however, that the minister did not state that it was the intention of the government to change the first clause of the bill to an even greater extent than that. I listened with interest to the speech delivered

Without question the regulations and the interpretation of the regulations are being tightened up, and it is certainly much more difficult now to get what one might consider a borderline case passed by the department. While saying that, however, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that in the past I have found the members of the board of review very co-operative; and after explaining certain new factors in regard to a particular case that may have been brought to my attention, on numerous occasions I have been successful in getting the application reconsidered and finally getting payment made.

speechtext:
In looking at the amounts that are paid from time to time I find that they are large, and they have been large over the last few years because there has been widespread crop failure. But the payment to any individual farmer is a very small one.
The Minister of Agriculture himself has said many times in the past that it is so small as to pay only the grocery and the clothing bills. The point is that thousands of farmers in western Canada, when they have a series of crop failures over a few successive years, must get assistance somewhere, and I think it is much better that they get assistance in the form of a cheque that they can use as they themselves see fit, than forcing them back on the relief rolls, as was our experience in the 1930's. The point is that if this act were withdrawn there would be no saving in money when we consider the amount that the various provincial governments and the federal government would have to pay in assisting people who have successive crop failures.
I do not want to leave the impression that all of this bill is not of value. Certainly the second clause is a good one. A week ago in respect to the second clause of the bill the Minister of Agriculture said that it was something that most hon. members thought a year ago should have been done when the legislation was before the house. I want to point out to him that last year in the committee on agriculture I moved a motion which was almost identical with the second section of the bill. My motion read as follows:
Where a section of land lies within an ineligible township and has a side that lies alongside an eligible township or is a section which lies alongside an eligible section or a corner of which touches the corner of an eligible township or an eligible section, such section of land shall be eligible for award as though it were a complete township.
The section in the bill reads as follows:
Where a block of contiguous sections of land within an ineligible township having an area of not less than one-sixth of the township and a side that lies along the boundary of an eligible township is determined by the board to have an average yield
Prairie Farm Assistance Act of eight bushels of wheat or less per acre, such block of sections of land shall be eligible for award as though it were a complete township.
I say that my motion and this clause are identical. But when my motion was moved in the agriculture committee last fall I found that all of the Liberal members voted against it. Therefore when the Minister of Agriculture says that last year most of the members of parliament supported this new clause I think he should say more specifically that members of the C.C.F. and the Social Credit parties, who voted for the motion, are the people who supported this particular clause.
Last Friday the Minister of Agriculture stated, as he did again this afternoon, what might be considered his interpretation of the first clause of the present bill. He said, as appears on page 2430 of Hansard'.
The people who have title to their land or have it under agreement of sale, though they may not have clear title-that is, the people who own their land in the sense that land is owned all across the country-are entitled to payment under the terms of this act. But if such a person or some other person goes on a piece of submarginal land and takes a cultivation lease, with the land still belonging to the government, whether it be this government, a provincial government or a municipal government, the amount is not payable on that land.
If that is the intention of the first section, then why does it not read that way? Why does the first section say that any new cultivation leases let by provincial governments on submarginal land will no longer be eligible for payment? Instead of that the section says that provincial lands, with the exception of lands held by veterans under the Veterans Land Act, and held as co-operative farms, as the minister said this afternoon, will not be eligible for payment.
I hope it is the intention of the minister through this section to try to get only submarginal lands removed from the provisions of the act, and that that is the extent of his intention. I am afraid however that by leaving the section as it now stands we are more apt to get a greater amount of submarginal lands under cultivation and eligible for payment under the act.
I say that for this reason, that under the present lease policy of the Saskatchewan and Alberta governments, those two governments can determine whether or not a farmer shall cultivate his lease, or use it for grazing. But if pressure results from this bill-if it passes in its present form-and is exerted on various provincial governments, to the point where they may abandon their present lease policy, and do what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has suggested, namely, sell their provincial lands, then of course there will be no control over the type of use to which the land is put. A farmer, if he can buy provincial

Prairie Farm Assistance Act land, after having purchased it can break it up, even if it is a very light soil; and he will be eligible for prairie farm assistance under the bill as it now stands.
In other words this bill has absolutely nothing to do with submarginal lands, and the taking of such lands out of wheat production. It is directed only at the land policy and the lease policy followed by the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Should those governments decide to sell that land, and if in the future, as has happened in the past when crown land has been sold, the farmers buying such land should undertake a huge obligation in the way of debt, then those farmers can no longer afford to carry on proper cultural practices.
If a farmer gets a cultivation lease over a thirty-three year period he will say, "Now I have some security. I am going to farm this land for the next thirty-three years in a way which will permit me to get the greatest possible return over that period." But if the same farmer has the same piece of land, but with a heavy debt on it, he will say, "I will farm this land in the next two or three years and, by the grace of God and some rain, I may get a couple of bumper crops and pay off my mortgage." The chances are that he will put a great deal more into wheat production, and continuous wheat production, with the end result after a few years that he has a greater number of crop failures, and consequently would be eligible for the bonus.
From the information I have been able to obtain, the Saskatchewan government is most careful in its leasing policy not to allow a cultivation lease on a piece of submarginal land in grass. A provincial government has just as great a stake in proper methods of agricultural practice as has the Minister of Agriculture or the federal government. If a provincial government follows a policy which results in the misuse of land, then of course they are going to be called upon from time to time to advance seed and to advance relief to the people within that province.
I have figures here from the department of agriculture in Saskatchewan which show that in that province there is just a little more than 5,000,000 acres under grazing lease. The province has control of some 800,000 odd acres in addition to that, which is not under cultivation, making a total amount of provincial land not under cultivation of 5,800,000 acres.
Then, the provincial crown lands leased on the basis of cultivation lease amount to a little more than 640,000 acres. In other words, just 10 per cent of all the crown lands in Saskatchewan are under cultivation lease.


Ninety per cent cannot be brought into wheat production. Of the 10 per cent that is under cultivation lease, 472,000 acres have been let for veteran settlement, with the approval of the Department of Veterans Affairs in Ottawa, and that 472,000 acres will be eligible for prairie farm assistance. So that this leaves a net of 169,000 acres in Saskatchewan under cultivation by civilian lease which will be denied payment of the bonus under this legislation.
In other words the lease policy of the Saskatchewan government has been so good that only two and one-half per cent of all crown lands can be affected by this amendment. The government of that province has been most careful to see that no cultivation lease is let on submarginal land, so that the amount of submarginal land in wheat production will be increased.
If the Minister of Agriculture wants the type of bill he has said on two or three occasions he would like to have, then he should say that in the future if any provincial government lets a new cultivation lease on submarginal land, then on such submarginal land prairie farm assistance payments will not be made.

This is what the minister said, as reported at page 2434 of Hansard:
But we do want to put this legislation in shape whereby no one can come into this House of Commons and say, "You are paying money out on submarginal lands which are owned by a government and should be under pasture"; this government is prepared to put it under pasture for the common good and someone deliberately goes on it

and gets a lease, and makes it impossible to do that. I do not think the House of Commons wants us to pay to continue that.
The minister there said they are going on pasture land and putting it under cultivation, and then they are getting P.F.A.A. payments, and that is what he wants to stop. Yet if the government is going to treat, as I believe it is not justified in treating, all provincial lease land on this basis, why does not the government include mortgage company land? Why does not the government include Canadian Pacific land and Hudson's Bay Company land that is under lease? Instead this legislation is directed at the provincial governments. There is no incentive, and no public responsibility imposed on companies like the Canadian Pacific or the Hudson's Bay Company with regard to a proper land utilization program. They lease their lands in such a way as to get the greatest possible amount of revenue and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is doing nothing about their leases. But in Saskatchewan, where in my opinion the government has a sound agricultural policy and has not allowed submarginal land to go into wheat production, the minister is removing all crown land from the provisions of the act while at the same time forcing farmers on that land to continue to pay one per cent into the fund year in and year out.
If the Minister of Agriculture is anxious to take submarginal land out of cultivation, I should like to show him a map I have here put out by his own department showing where submarginal land is to be found. The Department of Agriculture has paid hundreds of thousands of dollars to find where the submarginal land is and all the minister needs to do in this part of Saskatchewan is to take this map and declare that the yellow areas will not be subject to prairie farm assistance. If he does that he will be taking submarginal land out of the provisions of this act and perhaps out of wheat production altogether.
We need a proper land utilization policy which can be brought about only by co-operation between the federal, provincial and municipal governments as well as the people in the local communities. That land utilization policy would have to include increased areas under irrigation as well as increased acreages under grass. If a policy like that were followed the submarginal land could be taken out of production. Under such a policy farmers who are now on submarginal land could be given an economic unit either in the area in which they now live or in some other part of the province.
I submit that by the present bill the Minister of Agriculture is making a political football out of the P.F.A.A. when he tries
Prairie Farm Assistance Act to force Alberta or Saskatchewan to abandon its land policy. I am glad that the bill is to be referred to the agriculture committee and I hope that that committee will call the minister of agriculture for Saskatchewan or the deputy minister. We can then find out whether the Saskatchewan government has been allowing cultivation leases on submarginal land.
I think it is time the federal government and the provincial government got together to work out a policy which would be in the interests of the people in that part of Canada, which would include a proper land utilization program as well as a proper soil conservation program. Even while that is being done we would have to continue the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. In my opinion it is a national disaster when large areas in western Canada have successive crop failures, just as the present disaster in Winnipeg and along the Red river is a national disaster.
I am happy that the federal government has seen fit to give assistance to those people in Manitoba who are facing such devastating loss. I believe that that is a national disaster and it calls for a national contribution. However, I believe that when a corp failure is experienced in large areas in Canada it should also be considered a national disaster. Because of that, not only should the Prairie Farm Assistance Act be continued; it should be expanded and improved.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act irregular shapes. I am sure that that amendment will receive the hearty approval of the farmers in western Canada.
Section 1 of the bill is the contentious section and the Minister of Agriculture referred to it as containing bad news when he spoke a week ago. I agree that submarginal land should be taken out of cultivation, but I do not agree that the declaring of lands leased from governments as being ineligible for payments will accomplish that result. Therefore I was glad to hear the minister state that it was the intention to exclude lands in those areas from the operation of this section.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on this bill. It must be admitted that so far this session I have not said very much. I feel that our main problem in the drought areas is irrigation, and it was my intention to speak on the first item of the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). Since this bill has been brought in, however, I feel it necessary to say a few words, particularly in view of the statement by the minister this afternoon and in view of section 1 of the bill.
In his statement this afternoon the minister referred to the special areas. In the southeastern part of my province, particularly in my constituency, only a very small portion of the land is in these special areas. No doubt the minister knows that district quite well; that is the area north of the British block and from Empress along to Iddesleigh and Buffalo. That is in the special area, but the larger part of my constituency is in local


improvement districts. This afternoon the minister referred particularly to the special areas. If this bill goes through in its present form many farmers in local improvement districts are going to be disqualified from the bonus. It must be realized that in the local improvement districts many farmers are leasing land from the department of municipal affairs or the department of lands and mines.
I have had some experience along this line. The last municipality near Medicine Hat to go broke was M. D. 92, which was called Excelsior. It was turned over to the department of municipal affairs, and as an inspector of that department I held that area. So I feel I know a little about local improvement districts in my province. In that municipality, as in many other local improvement districts that I held, land went through tax sales. That land might have been homesteaded thirty or forty years ago, but through no fault of their own the farmers were forced into arrears of taxes, particularly in the thirties. Of course if a farmer was residing on land that went through tax sale he was protected to the extent that he could lease that land from the government. If crop conditions changed, or if his financial circumstances improved, he had the opportunity of consolidating the arrears of taxes that had accumulated on his land. He received the usual discount of up to 25 per cent, and paid the current taxes and arrears over a period of five years, after which that land was redeemed in his name. If he was not able to do that the department of municipal affairs leased that land to him on a crop share basis.
In those years the arrangement was that one-fourth of the crop went to the department, and that share was applied against the arrears of taxes on the land. If at the end of five years he was able to pay off all his arrears he got title to the land. If on the other hand crop conditions did not improve and he was not able to pay his consolidated taxes, he could lease that land. Title was taken by the government, and eventually the land was turned over to the department of lands and mines. When that happened the land was leased back to the farmer; and many of those leases are still in effect today. That is the position of a number of farmers east of the city of Medicine Hat. I know of one farmer in particular who homesteaded his land forty years ago. It is quite true that he does not have title to that land today, that he is still leasing it from the department of lands and mines; but many people who have been in

this country for sixty and seventy years have no title to any property, whether urban or rural.
Under this act that man who is living on his homestead will be disqualified in respect to this assistance. There is to be an amendment to deal with these special areas, but what is to happen to the farmers residing in the local improvement districts? If the minister had mentioned particularly the special areas in Alberta it might have been entirely different, but he referred to the special areas in general.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
If the payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act are to be confined to lands that are owned, we are going to make a big mistake. As the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) mentioned, there are many quarter-sections, as well as sections, in that area that are owned by the Hudson's Bay Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway. Some of the lands are owned by speculators who have it rented. It seems to me that if the government intends to disqualify government owned lands, it would only be fair to disqualify anyone who owns land unless he lives on the land and farms it. It seems to me that is a fair proposition. I certainly agree with the statement made by the member for Assiniboia.
It must be realized also that the policy of the Alberta department of lands and mines is that no more land should be put under cultivation. After being an inspector and assessor with the department of municipal affairs for ten years, I feel that I know fairly well what is going on in the area. As I said, the department of lands and mines feels that no further land should be put under cultivation. Anyone leasing land from the department today, even under a grazing lease, can only get a permit to put small areas under cultivation for feed purposes. When I say "for feed purposes", I think the minister understands what I mean. In the drought area there may be what we call a slough, which may be flooded in the spring but perhaps dries up by the end of May. This enables the farmer to plant an area of ten or fifteen acres for feed purposes. The department of lands and mines will not allow a farmer to grow any wheat on that land for sale; it must be for feed for his stock.
We are discussing a bill to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. We in the southeastern corner of the province believe we have another solution for the problem. We believe that if we utilize the water in that area, we can certainly relieve the dominion government of many of the obligations about which they are complaining today. This afternoon the minister stated that there had been a big increase in the amount paid out under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act during the last few years. I am sure that no one knows better than the Minister of Agriculture why those moneys have to be paid out. I may say that none of the farmers enjoy receiving the prairie farm assistance payments; they do not like being what you might term relief recipients any more than any of us would like to be on relief. Many of the farmers in the area of which the minister spoke this afternoon believe that the solution lies in the utilization of the water running through that
2666	HOUSE OF
Prairie Farm Assistance Act area. If that is done prairie farm assistance payments, so far as Alberta is concerned, will be eliminated.
The minister may not agree with that statement, but it has been proven in any area where you have irrigation, where you have trees or dams and you are distributing the water over the land, the atmosphere in that area is entirely different. All one has to do is to leave Medicine Hat on a day when it is about 110 in the shade and drive to Taber to notice the difference in the atmosphere. I am sure the minister has gone through that experience during the trips he has made through that country, unless he was too busily engaged to notice it at the time. It may be argued that it is not possible to bring water down to Medicine Hat or to the Saskatchewan boundary. To answer that question one only has to refer to the Meek report. If we consider that report of any value, we must agree that water can be brought to Medicine Hat.
I should like to tell the minister that I appreciate what the dominion government is doing in building the St. Mary's dam. A lot of good work is being carried on there, and it is work which I am sure will benefit a large area of southern Alberta. As I have said, after studying the Meek report one must agree that water can be brought to Medicine Hat. If we have that water I am sure the farmers in that area will know how to distribute it. Some officials may claim it is not possible to carry water from 150 to 175 miles without a great deal of evaporation; that it would not be economical to do so. According to the report I have just mentioned, if dams are constructed in that area, it is quite feasible. If it is not, I am sure that water can be pumped out of the south Saskatchewan river and that area can be made into a productive one. We realize, of oourse, that to pump water out of any river is perhaps more expensive than the canal system. But I would also remind the house that we have natural gas in the Bow island area, and natural gas could be used to work those engines required to pump water. We have heard a great deal about natural gas during the last two years; and natural gas can be used profitably in our irrigation systems. If it was not for natural gas in the vicinity of Medicine Hat we would not have many of the market gardens we have today. All along that river every market gardener has his own gas well.
Many hon. members in this house do not realize today that power is supplied by natural gas for the engines that are used for pumping water out of the south Saskatchewan river to irrigate these lands. That is


why Medicine Hat is considered to be one of the best corn-growing areas in western Canada. I may have a few laughs from across the floor, but we do not mind that. I should like hon. members to come up and see what we have and what we have done with natural gas and irrigation. That is why I say that if the dominion government believes that we are unable to bring water down from the St. Mary river dam to Medicine Hat, we can certainly pump it from the south Saskatchewan river and irrigate thousands of acres.
There are many projects in the same position in western Canada. We all realize that. We have the St. Mary-Milk river project, the Bow river development project and the Red Deer diversion project. In Saskatchewan, you have the south Saskatchewan project. That of course may cost considerably more money than will our projects in Alberta. But when that is feasible, why should not every one of those projects be made financially possible? There is no excuse whatever, except for one thing; and that is what it is going to cost the government to put it in. We realize that we must have a larger population in our western provinces, particularly Saskatchewan and Alberta. That is one of our solutions. If we develop these irrigation projects, we are doing a great deal not only for Canada but for many other countries from which we can get immigrants.
I believe that the time has arrived when these irrigation projects must be given consideration. We should not only consider the bill before us but we should consider what can be done to eliminate the bill; I think that is more important than the bill itself. If we are going to develop our natural resources as we should, why should not the government of Canada and the provincial governments put in our irrigation systems?
I have refrained from saying anything about irrigation this session, as the minister knows. I have been waiting for him to make a statement in connection with two projects which affect my constituency particularly.

speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will save any remarks I have to make on irrigation until the minister's estimates are before us.
