Louder.

You will hear me before I am through, so don't worry. I feel that on the first item of the Department of Agriculture we can give a general review of agricultural conditions in the country. I have discussed irrigation on other occasions in the house, and I want to say a few words about that subject before I resume my seat. I do not want to say anything in the house that would in any way embarrass either the dominion government or the provincial government before the international joint commission meets, but I do think I should say a few words on irrigation, and what it would mean not only to Alberta but to Canada as a whole.
Before dealing with irrigation I want to read an editorial regarding agriculture which appeared in the Medicine Hat News. I presume, Mr. Chairman, I shall be in order when
Supply-Agriculture
I read it. The editorial is entitled: "Pie-in-the-Sky Aggie Economics" and reads as follows:
Federal government representatives, ten of them, are tramping about the country on a mission to induce housewives to buy more dairy products, particularly milk and butter.
I want my hon. friends across the way to be sure to listen to this. I continue:
Medicine Hatters were given the treatment this week. We could think of other ways in which such time and money could be more profitably expended, even in a public service endeavour.
The urging of greater consumption of food staples, without the medium of greater purchasing power, is the nonsense of pie-in-the-sky economics.
I am sure all hon. members know that. The editorial continues:
No mother would have to be told to buy more dairy products if she had the money in her budget to do so. The sensible alternative to such hocum is a free Canadian market in basic products. We have little sympathy with grumbling over $1 beefsteak and 60-cent butter, or any other exorbitant price demand, when it is realized that consumers have the solution within their own grasp-boycott buying.
I presume the Medicine Hat News supports the Minister of Agriculture. I continue:
As long as shoppers are willing to pay the piper, then the tune will be called by the producers.
As I said, this editorial appeared in our local paper. Apparently today the Department of Agriculture have men going around the country, and ten of them were in Medicine Hat trying to convince the housewives that they should buy more dairy products. I am sure that today the housewives are buying all the dairy products that their incomes will permit them to. Whether that statement is true I do not know. The Minister of Agriculture knows and will tell us about it.
When I was home during the Easter recess I talked to many farmers in that area, and I must say that the wheat-growing farmers were rather discouraged about the new price they were to receive for their wheat. These farmers feel that during the war they contributed perhaps more to the economy of this country than anyone else by selling their wheat at a loss of perhaps $500 million or $600 million. That is the loss that was suffered by the farmers of western Canada. These farmers realize, and especially those in the southern part of the province where we have a drought area and have to depend a lot on prairie farm assistance, that their income is not very high.
Some hon. members may argue that there is one solution, namely, to leave wheat growing alone and grow coarse grains. Everyone in the house should know that in these drought areas wheat will withstand more drought than any other grain. That is a well

Supply-Agriculture
known fact. The farmer who may harvest six to eight bushels of wheat to an acre and has a field of oats and barley alongside it will not harvest any coarse grains. That is certainly well known in the area from which I come, and that is one reason why the farmers of that area are perturbed over the price of wheat for the coming crop year.
It is also realized that we need irrigation in that country. I want to refer to one small project to show what can be done in some small areas with the assistance of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the provincial government. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act men have done wonderful work. All of us must agree with that. It is true that it has cost a considerable amount of money. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has done very well in areas in which they have gone to build dams for small irrigation projects and dug-outs for stock watering purposes.
There is one project that I want to refer to particularly, namely, the Ross creek irrigation scheme. It is a scheme within twenty miles of Medicine Hat, in which the water is diverted from a creek and put into what might be called a natural reservoir. During the run-off this year the reservoir was filled to a depth of about fifteen feet in an area that covered about four hundred acres. Any time you have an area of four hundred acres in western Canada covered to a depth of fifteen feet of water you have something that is really worth while. I may say that perhaps the farmers who are going to utilize this water may not get so much benefit out of it this year. They are storing the water for benefits that they will receive next year. The land I refer to has been eligible for drought bonus for the last seven years, since 1942. We are going to have an irrigated area of perhaps 2,500 acres where the farmers can raise feed for their stock and grain of any kind, as well as all kinds of vegetables, Through the instigation of a man who was with P.F.R.A. at one time, and who is well known to the Minister of Agriculture-I am referring to Mr. Henry Cavan of Dunmore-much has been done to promote that project. He, along with Frank McCleay, worked on the project for several years. Now they have something to show for their efforts.
That is something that can be done in many areas of southeastern Alberta. So far as a general policy of irrigation is concerned, I should be very happy to have the minister tell the committee just what has occurred by way of irrigation in the past year. I have been watching the. press for announcements

stating that the government has reached an agreement with the Canada Land and Irrigation Company and the Alberta government with respect to the St. Mary-Milk river project. Thus far I have been disappointed.
It will be recalled that when in the last session I referred to various statements appearing in the press the minister replied that he did not publish either paper. With that I certainly agree. However, I feel that after discussing Bill No. 209, to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, we should be given some information as to what is going to be done to preserve our natural resources through the means of irrigation.
As I have said on many occasions, we have in the area of Medicine Hat the best land in Alberta, when it receives sufficient rainfall. I do not think anyone would contradict that statement. We are living in an area where our annual precipitation averages 12-70 inches and in some years is as low as 10 inches. In an area of that kind we are particularly interested in the promotion and development of our irrigation schemes.
I could speak at some length on this subject, dealing with what we could produce on those lands, the number of settlers we could care for and what it would mean to the economy of Canada. However, I do not think I should do that at the present time. On the other hand I feel consideration should be given by the federal and provincial governments to extending the existing projects in that area.
I appreciate what the Minister of Agriculture has done, and realize that he is up against some difficulties in promoting irrigation in southern Alberta. I know there are certain interests in eastern Canada that are opposed to the dominion government's spending large amounts of money in the development of irrigation on our western plains. May I say to those who would oppose such projects that the farmers and all others in western Canada have done their part in assisting to keep some of those who now criticize western Canada.
I have here many editorials which have appeared in some of the eastern newspapers in which easterners are critical of the development of our irrigation projects. I do not think it is necessary to read these to hon. members, because every hon. member must realize that when one part of Canada is helped, all of Canada is helped. That has been brought to our attention with great fcrce in the last month when two areas in Manitoba have been flooded. Those farmers will not have an opportunity to sow a crop this year; if they do, it will produce only feed. We

also have in mind the disastrous fires at Rimouski and Cabano in Quebec, and extend to those people our sincere sympathy.
Those of us in the dried-out areas of western Canada believe that the people of Canada generally have the same sympathy for us when we have a crop failure. And so it is in this spirit that I say to the Minister of Agriculture and other members of the federal government that everything should be done to bring about increased production on our great western plains.
One of the greatest mistakes we make is in our reference to the Palliser triangle. The time has long since passed when we should refer to western Canada in that way. As John Fisher said in a most able broadcast last fall from Lethbridge, it is time the people of Canada forgot about the Palliser triangle and got together to develop our land as one country.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock?
No.

I made the suggestion only because of the example set by other hon. members who have done the same thing. In rising to speak in connection with the first item in the agricultural estimates I realize that some hon. members may wonder why a member from a province with such a reputation for its fisheries should speak on agriculture. The fact is that agriculture is of great importance to Newfoundland. I hold in my hand a copy of the "Industrial Survey of the Resources of the Province of Newfoundland", prepared by Donald, Ross and Company, Montreal, for the Newfoundland industrial development board, and it was a great pleasure to me to find that in this report agriculture is stressed as being of great importance in the economy of the island. Dealing with that subject the writer says:
Farming, while on a comparatively small scale, occupies an important place in the economy of the island as the produce is largely grown for home consumption; whereas the other basic industries, fishing, pulp and paper and mining, produce almost exclusively for export.
During the past nine years Newfoundland has been riding the crest of a wave caused by the coming of Americans and Canadians who built large military and naval establishments in the country, and also because of the fact that high prices were received for the products of our fisheries, mines and forests which were exported. I felt somewhat doubtful of the position which I had always maintained when I saw these industries going ahead so fast and our people finding such easy money in working therein. I felt that
Supply-Agriculture
in neglecting agriculture to work in those industries some of our people were really neglecting their own best interests. In the past few months we have noticed that the fishing industry is not as reliable for a country's economy as a well-balanced agriculture. Next week a conference will be held in Ottawa attended by representatives of the salt cod fishing interests to discuss what can be done to market the balance of the 1949 catch and what they are going to do about fishermen who have refused to fish during the coming season.
It has been my belief that agriculture occupies the same place in Newfoundland as it does in other parts of Canada. In my opinion it is the most important industry, and I believe the early settlers realized that. When John Guy came to Newfoundland in 1610 he made an attempt to sustain his small colony by the produce taken from the soil. Unfortunately the attitude of the British government was to discourage both agriculture and colonization so that it was not until 1813 that land was first granted for agriculture.
Within a few short years after that date all the available land around St. John's was taken up. It must be remembered that at that time there were no roads in the country; there was no means of communication except by water. In a comparatively short time many fine farms were built up around St. John's, one by Governor Cochrane, the first governor after we were granted representative government in 1832. Roads followed as the result of the farm development policy. One farm was established in a place called Mount Pearl, called after the gentleman who established it, Sir William Pearl, I believe. Within the past ten or twelve years an experimental farm was set up on that very place which has now been taken over by the federal government. We expect that many experiments Will be carried on there which will be of great benefit to the country.
Unfortunately the story of agriculture in Newfoundland has been in a minor key. The economy of the country has been largely controlled by the strong mercantile and fishing interests. For hundreds of years the fish merchants made millions of pounds out of the fisheries and then often retired with their accumulated profits to England and spent nothing upon the development of the country. It was not until 1904 that the first paper mill was established. Prior to that time the interior of the country had hardly been touched.
In 1908 the first attempt was made to establish an experimental farm when the

Private Bills-Divorce
prime minister of that day, Sir Robert Bond, who himself operated a profitable farm at a place called Whitbourne, established the first experimental farm near St. John's. Unfortunately he was defeated in the election of 1909 and the government that followed placed a lawyer in charge of the department of agriculture with the result that within a year the place was sold and the experiments abandoned. I trust the Minister of Agriculture will sympathize with the misfortunes of the people of Newfoundland when a policy such as that was carried out.
I believe he and his advisers should know that Professor Zavitz, who had quite a reputation in this country, advised Sir Robert Bond on the setting up of that model farm; to have that work jettisoned proved a great handicap to the progress of agriculture in Newfoundland.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE THE ELIGIBLE AGE OP VOTERS FROM 21 TO 18
AMENDMENT TO REDUCE THE ELIGIBLE AGE OP VOTERS FROM 21 TO 18
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 11, to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1938 (age of voters).
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of this bill I shall be brief. I do not want to contribute to talking out the bill, and it is my hope that it may be dealt with during the one-hour period. My amendment would reduce the eligible voting age from 21 to 18 years. From time to time over the years various amendments to the Dominion Elections Act have been brought down. On various occasions parliament has decided that amendments were necessary in order to broaden the basis of the franchise and make each election as far as possible reflect the will of the people. Some provinces, notably Alberta and Saskatchewan, have already placed in their statutes a voting age lower than 21 years. In March, 1944, Alberta reduced the voting age from 21 to 19 years. In March of 1948 Saskatchewan reduced the eligible voting age for provincial elections from 21 to 18 years.
One of the main reasons that I feel parliament might well adopt this amendment is the fact that the standard of education is steadily improving. The present generation of young Canadians is better trained and better educated than any preceding generation. The 1941 census showed that the average education of Canadians 18 years of age was just over grade 10. In 1911 the census showed that the average education was just a little above grade 7. I believe the 1951 census will show a further improvement in educational standards and accomplishments.
It seems to me that with the present voting age of 21 years there is too great a gap between the time a student leaves high school and the time that student is likely to vote in an election. I think all political parties agree that for the proper functioning of a democratic system it is necessary and desirable that the youth of the country be interested in public affairs. So each political party represented in this house has its own youth organization. I am sure members of all parties will agree that it is most difficult now to get young people interested in Canadian affairs, and I think one of the reasons it is difficult is the fact that quite a number of years must elapse between the time a youth leaves high school and the time he is eligible to vote.
While anyone in Canada of the full age of 21 is eligible to vote in a federal election, that does not mean each person on reaching

Dominion Elections Act
the age of 21 can vote at that time, because federal elections usually come only once every four or five years. This means that most young Canadians must wait until they are 23 or 24 years of age before getting an opportunity to vote. Speaking for myself- and in this perhaps I am different from other hon. members-I did not have the opportunity to vote until I was 24. In that election I probably used bad judgment, along with many other people, in that I voted for myself. If I had been given the opportunity to vote in the 1940 election, when I was 19 years of age, I no doubt would have voted for someone else. In any case, if this house should decide to reduce the voting age to 18 it would mean that the average age at which young Canadians would in fact have the opportunity to exercise their franchise would be 20 or 21 years.
I believe that if the voting age were reduced all political parties and associations across the country interested in public affairs would have much greater success in getting young people into their organizations and in having them take an active interest in the civic, provincial, national and international affairs of the day. I am sure most youths leaving high school ask themselves what is the advantage in being associated with a political party or of interesting themselves in public affairs if they must wait five, six or seven years before getting an opportunity to vote. I believe that Canadian youth in our high schools today are getting a valuable training in democratic processes, and I think they would be more likely to maintain a continuing interest if they knew that at an early date they would have the opportunity to vote.
Along with that reason, as I mentioned previously, there is the fact that our young people today are the best educated perhaps of the young people in any country in the world. The fact that they have great ability and great intelligence is proven by the magnificent and heroic part played in the war by Canadian youths eighteen, nineteen and twenty years of age. They showed during that time that they were capable of taking the most advanced and intricate training in the armed forces; that they were able to operate skilfully the modern and complicated instruments of war. Our nation felt, and rightly so, that it was wise to spend $25,000 in the education of a navigator or a pilot. Our enemy learned that the teen-aged Canadian youth was a formidable opponent on the field of battle.
I believe that since it was the right thing at that time to give all members of the armed forces a vote in the election, even though they were in their teens, it is certainly right
and proper for the parliament of Canada to give youth who may be called to the colours a chance to exercise the vote in an election before that call might take place. While the effort achieved by young Canadians in the recent war left nothing to be desired, yet I believe young Canada has the right to a voice in public affairs when, at any time, it may be called upon to join the armed forces and be asked, in many cases, to make the supreme sacrifice in the defence of our democratic institutions. If our democratic institutions are worth the lives of young Canadians and I believe they are, then in peacetime those same young Canadians should have a voice in the affairs of our nation.
Because, Mr. Speaker, I believe Canadian youth is intelligent enough to cast a responsible ballot in an election, because Canadian youth has shown such great accomplishments in the armed forces during wartime, I would ask the house to support this bill.

Judging by their interest in public affairs, you may go into any high school or collegiate across this country where you have a group of eighteen to twenty-one year olds, and you will find they are as keen and as interested in public affairs as any other group of citizens. He is now twenty-two years of age, and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the attitude of that boy today is quite different from what it was when he was eighteen. Young men and young women of eighteen years are still at an impressionable age. Either they have just left school or have just begun work or entered college. As the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth (Mr. Kirk) has pointed out, they have been influenced by their teachers. They have also been influenced by their parents. All hon. members will agree that parental influence is one of the great virtues in this world; but on the other hand how many parents drill into the minds of their children the thought that they should vote just as their parents have always voted? That line of direction is not going to improve a country's voting.
Then, in the matter of influence exerted by schoolteachers, let me say at once that I have nothing but the highest regard and respect for the teaching profession. In fact, to my mind it is probably the most necessary
profession to be found in any modern civilized country. The fact remains however that among teachers, as among other groups in society, there are a few radicals who compose a very noisy minority. As in other phases of life, this noisy minority makes itself loudly heard, and its influence is out of all proportion to what it should be.
Eadical ideas can be taught more readily in schools than at any other time of life, simply because the boy or girl at the school is at the most impressionable age. I cannot help feeling that it takes at least three years after the young man or woman has left school to get, by means of the hard knocks in life, an appreciation of the realities of life.
I do not wish to repeat anything that has been said with respect to young men and young women. But as to young men and young women who have been enlisted or drafted into the armed services of Canada, we know that they are given the vote. As has been pointed out already, these young men and women, as they would be in schools, are under rigid discipline. They are accountable to their superior officers and in some instances are influenced so that they will vote as they are told to vote. It is unfortunate that this should be so, but I do not believe there is a member in the House of Commons who would deny the fact that an officer in the armed forces wields a tremendous amount of influence in respect of how the men under his command will cast their ballots.
I would doubt that permitting young men and women of eighteen to twenty-one years the right to vote would in any way prevent this country from entering another war. I should not think it likely that the influence of young people would so affect the policy of the government of Canada in respect of its external affairs that war would be avoided, so that those young people would never again be forced to fight in the armed services. I am afraid the argument used in that respect, where it is pointed out that young people could avoid armed service were they allowed to vote, is a weak one.
It was my good fortune at this session and the last one to have as my guests the students of no less than four schools from the county of Leeds. These were the students of two high schools and two continuation schools. In two of those schools mock parliaments have been organized. They have their own elected prime ministers and their own elected cabinets, and to a certain extent they have accepted the responsibility of maintaining student discipline. These young people are very keen about their parliament. One of their chief reasons for wishing to come to Ottawa has been to see how this House of

Dominion Elections Act Commons compared with their parliamentary attempts. Those students have been most interested spectators in the gallery, and they have left greatly impressed with the dignity of the house. The actual working of a democratic assembly has been brought home to them, and they have all agreed that they have learned something from having been here.
But, Mr. Speaker, of those two hundred students who visited here, some of whom were eighteen years of age, I have not heard [DOT]one ask that the voting age be reduced from twenty-one to eighteen. I have not such a closed mind that I would not agree this matter should be given further study; but I do not think the time is ripe for passing a bill of this kind. I heartily agree with the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth that this is a matter having a degree of importance sufficient to merit its being referred to a committee for further study, and for recommendation to the house.

I do not see why he does not carry that to its logical conclusion and raise the minimum voting age to seventy years. Then if only the old age pensioners were able to vote we might get a different kind of government than we have today. The fact of the matter is that we are hearing the same old argument that because somehow or another young people are different, they are not as responsible as we are.
I will confess that I am getting old enough that at times I have thought that about the younger generation, but I want to repeat what I said a few days ago, that any opinion I might have had along that line was dispelled for all time when I was home in Winnipeg last week. I say categorically, fully recognizing all the work that older people by the thousands have done, that if it were not for the boys and girls of twenty-one years and younger who are at work on the dikes in the Winnipeg area, Winnipeg would be under a lot more water than it is. These boys and girls of twenty-one years and under have shown a sense of real responsibility and I think we older people should give them the further responsibility of the right to vote.

Mr. Speaker, I perhaps am inspired or stimulated to speak this evening by what the last speaker has said. I cannot claim to be one of the younger members in this house, but I would like to think that I am not one of those who believe that young people should be dragooned by older people into what they should think. I believe that in our own party we should have more of them at work with us, and I am glad to think that we will be able to do it. I really rose to my feet because I think there is a danger of sentimentality taking [DOT]charge here. We must remember that there is such a thing as common sense. I echo almost every word said by the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth (Mr. Kirk). I was glad it was said by a schoolmaster because after all he should know young people better than we do.
I admire the heart of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), but I do not admire so much his head. It seems to me it is one thing to get young people interested, but the hon. member for York South really

got to the position where he was saying that there is nothing in experience. Those of us who are older do not think that there is too much in experience because we have made too many mistakes to flatter ourselves, but I do suggest that there is something in experience. When we go to the length of practically saying that there is not, I think we are becoming sentimental.
There is just one other thing I want to say. I think to use the army as an analogy is one of the most misleading things that could be done. I take second place to no one in my admiration of what many young boys of eighteen years or under did during the war. They did things that no one else in the world could have done. They were able to fly aeroplanes in a way that an older man could not; in fact they said that a man of twenty-five who was still in the air was practically in his grave.
But to say that because they make such splendid soldiers between the ages of eighteen and twenty-one years we should give them and all others of their age the vote seems to me to be just letting our feelings run away with us. I think the sober views expressed by the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth based on the wide experience of other countries should be considered. Why should we ignore the experience of other countries? Is it just an accident that those countries which have shown stability, which is so lacking in this world, have not acceded to the suggestion of an extreme minimum age for voting?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE THE ELIGIBLE AGE OP VOTERS FROM 21 TO 18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two arguments in favour of reducing the age for voting from twenty-one years to eighteen, and one cannot be disproved. When you conscript men to fight then it is not as important that they should cast a vote, even for myself, on election day as it is to have to go to fight for their country. The other argument advanced is that, when we allow people of eighteen years to get married they should be allowed to vote, and, if that is admitted, we are considering it is not as important to cast a vote as it is to get married.
That argument does not hold water because I find on our order paper many bills for the relief of John Robert from Mary Anne and so on. I do not think people should get married at eighteen years of age. I did not have enough sense then and perhaps I have not yet.

Mr. Chairman, at the six o'clock recess I was referring to the first experimental or model farm which had been established near St. John's in 1908 by Sir Robert Bond, who was prime minister at the time. It was his idea to establish farming as a vocation in Newfoundland and it was for that purpose that he set up this experimental farm. However, it was his successor's idea that fishermen-farmers should be encouraged, but I have always thought that there was room for both. I may say that the minister of agriculture in the government returned in 1909 was a lawyer. As everyone who has been in Newfoundland realizes, while there are certain areas suitable for large-scale farming, there are many other places where people are crowded together, where the men carry on fishing but there is still room for little gardens to supplement their earnings from the sea.
The government that came into power in 1909 favoured the establishment of agricultural societies, and gave them grants on a fifty-fifty basis. These probably did some good, because they enabled the farmers or the fishermen-farmers to purchase seeds and equipment for their farms; but I think it is true to say that during the following ten years, up to 1919, not only did agriculture not progress in Newfoundland, it actually declined.
In that year a new government came into power, one member of which was a distinguished gentleman from Prince Edward Island who had a traditional knowledge of farming which he proposed to put into operation in Newfoundland. He set up another model farm. I shall not go into the history of the department of agriculture during those sad four years for Newfoundland. Suffice it to say that the government resigned in 1923, after having been re-elected that very year, and the succeeding government disposed of the model farm by auction, lock, stock and barrel, so there was no act on the statute books of Newfoundland dealing with agriculture except a sheep preservation act, and that was not carried out. That sheep preservation act, I may say, set up a fund to compensate the owners of sheep that had been destroyed by dogs. It has always been a big question, especially in certain areas of Newfoundland, whether it is preferable to have sheep or dogs, and I think the dogs have won out.

Supply-Agriculture
In 1926 Sir Robert Bond died and in his will, like Julius Caesar, left his property to the province. He had a fine farm consisting of some ten square miles of cleared land and fine woodland right on the railway and at a central point in the peninsula of Avalon. This was bequeathed to the people of Newfoundland to be used as a model farm forever; but what did the government of the day do? It declined to accept the bequest. I take pride now in the fact that I was one of the very few, if there were any others, who stood up in the House of Assembly and advocated that the government should accept that bequest and operate the property as a model farm. The government was afraid to do that, however, because between 1919 and 1923 the model farm had been such a hopeless failure. The real reason the government did not take that property and work it as a farm was that it did not have a proper appreciation of the value of agriculture in the economy of Newfoundland.
In 1932, when our country fell upon very difficult times and we were in the throes of a financial crisis, a land development association was formed under the promotion of the president of Memorial University college, a distinguished educationist; and that association did valuable work, without any outside assistance of any kind, in encouraging people who were unemployed to work on allotments. It assisted many people throughout Newfoundland to obtain seed and fertilizer. Especially was that so in Bell island, where the miners were working only two days a week. I was a member of that land development association, and with our assistance those miners purchased seed and fertilizer, and were able to produce fine crops from their gardens. I may add that there is very good soil on Bell island. They had an exhibition that year which I believe would have done credit to any place of the same size in Ontario or Quebec. That exhibition opened the eyes of many people who attended it.
Then when the commission government came in, in 1934, they investigated what should be done. They had before them the Amulree report setting out the history of agriculture, as well as that of other industries; and Mr. Lodge, who was commissioner for public works, took it upon himself to make a private investigation. I well remember hearing him say that of all the industries he had examined the one he felt would give the greatest results from the application of artificial stimuli was agriculture. Unfortunately, however, when he went to apply these artificial stimuli he went to the wrong place. Where did he go but to a boggy area in the rear of the very property of Sir Robert Bond which the government had refused
[Mr. Browne (St. John's West) .1
back in 1926? As a result the commission government had an extremely difficult task in trying to bring about land settlement in that area, though they did take unemployed people from St. John's and put them on the land there.
That was a very expensive experiment. Nevertheless I believe the government learned a great deal from it, and as a result they went on to further experiments, and to establish settlements at such places as Markland, Midland, Vinland, Lourdes, where a combination of farming, logging and fishing made the experiment very successful, and Brown's Arm, where good guidance brought about the same result. Later the experience gained in these experiments was utilized in the settlement of veterans in the valley of the Upper Humber river. The commission government also brought to Newfoundland Mr. McCharles who was a splendid director of agriculture. Unfortunately for Newfoundland he enlisted as soon as war broke out and we lost the benefit of his services. We had another director of agriculture, Mr. Gillis, who studied at Truro agricultural college, but I am sorry to say he retired the other day and went back to farming. The commission government gave bonuses for clearing the land; it instituted a survey of soils in different parts of the country, and it assisted those interested in clearing land by the use of tractors.
Now a new era has begun with confederation; but though the director of agriculture resigned, as yet no one has taken his place. Nor was there any mention of agriculture in the budget presented by the premier the other day. I was sorry to see that, because I knew he had carried on experiments in farming himself. Last session the Minister of Agriculture, during the course of a debate on the rehabilitation of farms in western Canada, while dealing with the question of marshlands in New Brunswick said he would like to go to Newfoundland to see if he could do anything of that nature there. Well, I am very glad to learn that the minister hopes to go to Newfoundland. I trust he will come, but I hope he will not keep that subject uppermost in his mind. There are other things I believe would be of greater service and would bear fruit more quickly than the reclamation of marshlands. What I think we need in Newfoundland at the present time, if 1 may venture to say so, is an extension of the school of agriculture that was created by the commission government at its experimental farm which the federal government is now taking over. We also need illustration stations similar to the two hundred or more stations scattered across Canada. I believe there are ten in Prince Edward Island, and

on that basis I think we should have at least thirty in Newfoundland. In any case I hope it will be possible to have a good many.
We want farming to be elevated. We want the public to realize that farming is a very important vocation and that those who pursue it should be honoured and not belittled. We want those who are interested in settling the land to be given assistance in clearing the land. I know that during the last couple of years it has been impossible for a man to get the use of a tractor. There were so many people looking for a tractor to clear land that a man was told he would probably have to wait until next year to get his turn. There were not enough tractors available to enable the land to be cleared. I think that is regrettable.
We want exhibitions to be encouraged. I am sure that the minister would agree that exhibitions are a most valuable adjunct to the promotion of agriculture. We have local exhibitions in Newfoundland, but for many years now we have had no provincial exhibition, and we need provincial exhibitions. Our people ought to be encouraged to take part in the Canadian national exhibition. I remember reading in Prouse's history that one hundred years ago oats and barley from Newfoundland had been sent over to Edinburgh, and won first prizes in, an agricultural exhibition. I believe barley can be grown in Newfoundland as well as in Canada. I certainly hope to see the minister go to Newfoundland, so that he can see for himself what the conditions are. I think he can gain more knowledge by a trip around the province than he can by listening to reports from me or anyone else. I believe he will be able to ascertain what our problems are, and he will see that there are these areas suitable for large-scale farming, as well as those smaller areas in which people can be encouraged to grow the food that they need.
This report which I have is worth studying. It says that people can grow the essential foods in Newfoundland, and can grow them in greater quantity than they are doing today. A study I made a couple of years ago as to the production of potatoes and turnips in Newfoundland showed that forty years ago we were producing twice as much as we are today. Even a study of the figures in this book will illustrate that no progress has been made in the production of vegetables, beef or milk, and there is every reason for progress to be made. This study was made within the past year, and shows that there are about six suitable areas for large-scale farming operations. Principally, I want to see farming on a small scale, such as you have in the province of Quebec, encouraged. Whether or not the
Supply-Agriculture
people are paying income taxes, they are producing food which they need, and they have a little left over that they can sell in the markets for cash, with which they can buy other things.
Handicrafts have been encouraged in Newfoundland. We have the equivalent of your women's institutes, as I believe they are called. I am not sure of the name, but they are societies for the encouragement of handicrafts. In Newfoundland there are the Jubilee Guilds. There are about 120 of these, and the people do a certain amount of knitting and weaving. From the cloth that is woven, garments are made. Fine cloth has been woven in Newfoundland. In my humble opinion, Mr. Chairman, there is no field of endeavour upon which the success or failure of confederation will be more marked than in the field of agriculture. You cannot teach us much about how to conduct our fisheries. You can give us assistance when we find difficulty in marketing our catch, just as you give assistance to the farmer in western Canada who has difficulty in marketing his products. You cannot teach our fishermen much. They are just as brave and as resourceful and as intelligent as the fishermen of the other maritime provinces. Our industries, such as pulp and paper, have the best brains available, and our mining is well conducted. In regard to agriculture, however, we must take off our hats to the Canadian people. Here is an opportunity for the federal government, and for a man like the present Minister of Agriculture, who is an experienced farmer and an experienced minister of agriculture, to put agriculture in Newfoundland in its proper relationship to the other industries.
Before I conclude, Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer once again to this industrial survey of the resources of the province of Newfoundland. It is, of course, recognized that many parts of our country are not at all suitable for agriculture. The report says:
Nevertheless an expansion of agricultural production to supply a greater proportion of the home market should be possible. Any expansion in agriculture would materially improve the economic position of Newfoundland, reducing imports from the rest of Canada for which there are no offsetting exports.
Figures produced to me the other day show that Newfoundland exports $93 million worth of products, and it imports through its own ports, from places other than the provinces of Canada, $23 million worth of goods. This means that somewhere in the neighbourhood of $70 to $80 million is going to the other provinces of Canada, principally to buy foodstuffs, clothing, footwear and the other things we need, whereas the other provinces of Canada are only buying about $10 million worth of goods from us. So you see, there is

Suppl y-A griculture
an imbalance there that should be corrected by the province of Newfoundland producing more of the things it needs.
The report continues:
While climatic conditions do not favour the growth of cereal grains, the possibilities of expanding truck garden production, both in, the outlying communities and adjacent to the larger centres of population, seem reasonably good.
The writer of this report is not exaggerating when he says that.
If agricultural production is to expand, marketing procedures will have to be organized and adequate facilities such as storages, provided.
We suffer a great deal from the lack of storage. I do not believe there are any refrigerator cars in use in the province.
The proximity of the maritime provinces, particularly Prince Edward Island, with their established agriculture and relatively easy transport by water to the larger markets offers serious competition for local produce.
That is a matter that certainly needs investigating, but I understand the government is going to do that.
Combined with this is the geographical difficulty that the better agricultural land lies in the west, and the large market of the Avalon peninsula is in the east. Despite the difficulties, we believe an expanded and more prosperous agricultural industry can be developed. Among the main objectives should be larger farms, more modern methods of production, an educational program to promote higher fertility and greater yields, and a progressive marketing policy with adequate marketing facilities.
There is only one other thing I have to say, sir, and that is, should the officials of the Department of Agriculture make a survey of the situation in Newfoundland now, and then in three, four or five years' time make another survey, it would be possible to see what progress has been made. I shall judge them on what progress has been made during that time, and I believe other people will do the same.

Mr. Chairman, I take it that this is the correct place to raise with the Minister of Agriculture a question which has to do with the organization of his department. I no longer speak with any authority about agricultural matters in this house, but I should like to ask the minister one or two questions about organization.
As one would expect, one finds the Department of Agriculture fully organized. To my surprise however I find there is apparently an extraordinary amount of duplication of organization as between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce. In case the minister has not noticed this, I should like to draw it to his attention and ask him to explain what, on the

face of it, seems a most extraordinary duplication of effort. I have before me the government telephone directory for 1950, which I take it is accurate, and I will just read quickly the headings of the organizations of the Department of Agriculture as they appear.
First of all, there is livestock and poultry, that is in the Confederation building. Then, you have the plant products division, and from that one goes on to marketing services. There is a complete array of marketing services. Then, you turn over to the Department of Trade and Commerce, and you find what appears, on the face of it, as I said, a most extraordinary duplication. I shall just read a few instances of the various duplications and then the minister will no doubt explain to us how the duties are divided. I do not know whether one department takes one part of Canada and another takes another part of Canada, or whether one department deals with certain kinds of pigs and another department deals with another kind of pigs or how it is divided up; but at any rate, the minister will explain. I will just first of all point out the similarity in the general organization. Here we have livestock and poultry division under the Department of Agriculture; and there is quite an array there, by the way. There is sheep, cattle, swine, horses and so on. Then we turn over to the Department of Trade and Commerce and we find what they call the agricultural commodities branch, and under there we also find livestock and animal products; and going further under the Department of Agriculture we find the plant products division and we find somewhere poultry, of course. Then coming to the Department of Trade and Commerce we find the dairy and poultry products. Turning back to Agriculture we find plant products; and turning to Trade and Commerce we also find plant products there. There is an adequate array of officials in each department who, as I say, are dealing with this, and the minister will explain to us the division of duties between these parallel departments.
Then we go on and I think this is even more interesting. We go on to the marketing side of the organization and we find that the Department of Agriculture seems to be fully staffed over there in the Confederation building. It is not far away, I think, from the Department of Trade and Commerce. I think they are just next door and maybe they communicate with each other. One does not know. But under the Department of Agriculture there is first of all the marketing service with an array of officials there. We

go on further to the markets information section. No doubt that will be in the publicityline. Then we come to the consumer section, then to the agricultural economics division.
Then we come on really to the marketing proper and we find a whole series of divisions. They are very well equipped in the Department of Agriculture to do marketing. First of all there is the dairy products division in which there is an assistant director of marketing; then there is a general office, and there is a head clerk. Then we come down to dairy products grading and inspection service; and then a little later there is an array of officers there. Then we come to the marketing and merchandising service, and then there is the refrigeration service. Then we come to the fruit and vegetable division, and again there is an associate director of marketing. Coming on down there is a marketing and merchandising service. Then we come down to the livestock and livestock products division. Oh yes, there is a chief of agricultural marketing services. Then in the poultry division there is an assistant director of poultry marketing and so on. But I need not worry the committee with that. I just come now to the Department of Trade and Commerce, to show what an excellent service the Minister of Trade and Commerce has here, because he does not like to be left out of things, as we know. He gets into the transport department and all kinds of things where he has no business to be but where he likes to be; and I am amazed, I must confess, that the Minister of Agriculture apparently lets him keep on playing about in his department. But no doubt he will explain about that when the time comes. Here is the offering which the Minister of Trade and Commerce makes to us under the head of marketing. First of all, I should point out that he has an agricultural division. Before I come to that, there is an agricultural commodities branch which I have mentioned. As I pointed out a' few minutes ago it has a dairy and poultry products department, livestock and animal products, plants and products. Then we go on to the economic research and development branch. That I think is more general. I observe with interest there that they have a private and public investment department. I imagine that would interest the Minister of Finance. Then we go on to their marketing services. They have all kinds of marketing services, of course. They have an export division-
Which department is this?

in the Department of Trade and Commerce. It has excellent services. Then I come on

Then there is a crop section, special crops, livestock and animal products section, research and compilation section. Then we come on more particularly to merchandising.

find that in Trade and Commerce. That is in Agriculture. I could not find that in Trade and Commerce, but we may mention it to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I have no doubt he would oblige us with that too.
I want to go on to this marketing to show what an excellent service there is in the Trade and Commerce department in marketing. There is a whole page of it. You come to industry and merchandising division, and that is apt to fool you because you may not think it is agriculture. But if you read carefully through it you find the second heading is animal products section. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is again helping the Minister of Agriculture with his merchandising. Then you go on through. Here and there you find references to the information services and publicity sections. That is what you would expect. Then you come to external trade division, and I think that is nearly all.
As I said, I read these two lists of services which seemed so parallel. The Department of Agriculture, when I read it, seemed quite adequate, and I was surprised to find what appeared to be so fully a duplicate of the services in the Department of Trade and Commerce. As I said a moment ago, I should like to have an explanation of that. Whether the minister wishes to give it now or later, I do not know. That is not perhaps a matter of great consequence. But on the face of it I think we have here something which needs an answer, because we were assured by the Minister of Finance that there was no duplication and no waste. It may be that the Minister of Agriculture-who, I must say, has a gift for explanations which all of us may envy even though we cannot emulate it-can explain this situation. But if he can explain it, all I can say is that he can explain anything. I should like to know about it, and I should like to give him an opportunity now or later to explain why all these officers are in these two departments which seem to be doing the same thing, how they get along and how they arrange their duties.

It is not nearly as difficult as it sounds when my hon. friend discusses it from the telephone book.

First of all, I want to ask the minister this question, and I am sure he will allow me to do so. I want to ask if this is quite accurate, because I do not want it all blown away on the ground that it is inaccurate.
I suppose it is accurate; but people do not usually take the telephone book to explain what goes on in a department.
I will show it to the minister if he does not know about it.

The fact is a very simple one. The Department of Trade and Commerce promotes trade in all products that are produced in Canada, and promotes it outside Canada. That is what trade and commerce means. They are promoting the sale of all kinds of products in other countries. Naturally they have an organization which gathers information with regard to it and distributes that information in other countries. For example, they do not sell cars. They do not sell the products of our mines, particularly. They do not sell anything of that kind, except in the case of a product like wheat which they are now selling indirectly through the wheat board. They do not sell agricultural products either. But they do look over the whole world to find markets not only for agricultural products but for every other Canadian product; and in order to be able to look over the world for that purpose, they must of course have persons who are more or less experts in discussing the strong features of any product that we have to sell. We do not duplicate their service outside Canada. We have six men in Britain whom we call cargo inspectors, who are at the ports and whose chief job is to check the products that go from Canada to Britain to find out whether the gradings which are carried out in Canada are carried right through until the product is delivered on the other side. To that extent we have some men outside Canada, but they are very few.
The Department of Trade and Commerce has staffs that promote the marketing outside Canada. On the other hand the Department of Agriculture has charge of the marketing of farm products inside Canada. We mean by that the products which are delivered to the person who purchases inside Canada.
The reason, why the Department of Agriculture handled the agreements that were made with Great Britain during the war was that the products were delivered for the
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1	,
first time since the previous war, and I am not absolutely certain that they were delivered in any different way in the first war. Prior to the last war, in between the wars, and certainly prior to the first war, the delivery of products was made to a large extent on the other side of the' ocean. Quite often we paid the freight. When the last war started Britain undertook to take delivery because she had absolute control of the shipping on the seas. She took delivery of the products at the ports here, and so the Department of Agriculture took charge of the assembling of the products, having them delivered at Montreal, collecting the payment for them at Montreal, and from there on Canada had nothing more to do with them. Immediately the products were put on the ship, even if the ship was sunk in the middle of the Atlantic, Britain paid for them; we did not. It was that change in the manner of handling products which resulted in the Department of Agriculture assembling the products, selling them for delivery in that way, and then they went from there outside and we had nothing more to do with them. That is the real division as between the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Agriculture, namely, that we handle the gradings of all of the products that are purchased in so far as they are handled by Ottawa, and we handle the gradings in co-operation with the provincial governments.
How long has that division been in effect-since 1936?

It has been in effect for at least thirty years. It has been in effect ever since I knew anything about agriculture either provincially or federally, and it has always been in effect since I came here, which is fifteen years ago, and it was that way when I came. There is no question about that. The first dominion-provincial meeting that was held in Ottawa after I came here in 1936 had as one of its divisions an agricultural section. The whole task that was assigned to those who were gathered here was to remove any overlapping as between the dominion Department of Agriculture and the provincial departments. The general report at the end of the conference was that there was at least as little, and in most cases less overlapping in the Department of Agriculture than there was in any of the other departments. I am not talking now in the interests of the party to which I belong because that was within a few weeks after the present government took over from the Bennett government. The situation then was that there was no overlapping as between the provinces and the dominion.

I was asking about the division as between the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Agriculture.

The division as between
trade and commerce and agriculture was announced in the House of Commons by the prime minister in January, 1938.
That is the question I asked.
But there was nothing new about that either. It was just a recitation by the Prime Minister of what the situation had always been considered to be.
Oh, no.

There was a very marked
difference of opinion, which bears on something that the hon. member for Greenwood just said, namely, the long controversy that went on during the period that Mr. Bennett's government was in office between the then minister of trade and commerce, the late Mr. Stevens-[DOT]
Not the late.

I beg your pardon; Mr. Stevens, who was then minister of trade and commerce; and it did cause considerable hilarity not only in the house but outside it. They got out a blue book which was intended to cover agriculture; they distributed it throughout Canada and throughout the world. The agricultural critic on the opposition side of the house got up in the house and held the book up to indicate that the sow which had a litter of twelve pigs nosing around her turned out to be the male member of the species rather than the sow, and it was suggested that as a result of that probably trade and commerce was taking on too much of agriculture. As my hon. friend knows, that discussion went on in the period between 1930 and 1936, but in 1938 Mr. King finally made the division very plain as between the two. One had to do with trading outside Canada; the other had to do with merchandising inside Canada.
There is one part of the discussion that no one has ever been able to change or settle in the minds of people generally. Grain has always been under trade and commerce. Ever since we had a Canada Grain Act it has been under trade and commerce. It was not always called the Canada Grain Act. It had another name for a time, but what we know today as the Canada Grain Act was passed in 1900 or 1901. It was at the time when the production of grain on the prairies became an actuality. We had a farm organization in western Canada at that time headed largely by a gentleman who later became Senator Douglas. He along with the farm organization, the grain 55946-170
Supply-Agriculture
growers and others agitated for a grain act that would regulate the grading and handling of grain.
Just prior to that time the Laurier government had been formed, and as most hon. members know, Sir Richard Cartwright had been the financial critic in the house for a considerable period of time. It was thought by most people that when a new government was set up he would probably become minister of finance. He did not become minister of finance. Sir Wilfrid took a younger man in as minister of finance in the person of Mr. Fielding and he set up a department for Sir Richard Cartwright. That department had to do with matters of trade, customs and that kind of thing. Along with many other things that were put into it this new act having to do with the control of grain was put in when enacted. I think every minister of agriculture that we have ever had in Canada since about 1910 or 1912 has thought that it should be in the Department of Agriculture, but nobody else seems to think so, and so it remains the way it is. It is still in the Department of Trade and Commerce, and it is being carried on there partly because of the fact that most of our wheat is sold outside Canada. As the years went by there was a larger and larger percentage of it that had to be sold outside Canada. So that even the matter of grading, in so far as grain is concerned, is carried on in the Department of Trade and Commerce, as a result of the organization at that time; and it has continued that way to the present. The grading of every other farm product is looked after in the Department of Agriculture.
I have here the statement to which reference was made a moment ago. Perhaps I should read it, so that if it is required as a reference it will not be necessary to look it up in the Hansard of 1938. The question has been asked by the hon. member for Lake Centre as to when the announcement of policy was made, or the position taken. On January 31, 1938, Mr. King said this:
With respect to the consolidation of the department, that has been a matter of internal organization in the department, the minister managing his own department and arranging its affairs within the terms of the law.
So that there may be no mistake about the line of demarcation between the functions of the two departments, may I say what my understanding of it is-and I think it is correct. The marketing of agricultural produce in so far as it relates to Canada is a matter that belongs entirely to the Department of Agriculture. There can be no doubt about that. There are in Canada provincial departments of agriculture as well as the federal department, and it is necessary for the minister so far as the federal Department of Agriculture is concerned, to have supervision over the entire work of marketing throughout all parts of Canada. As Minister of Agriculture, he is equally interested in seeing that all agricultural commodities for sale in foreign

Supply-Agriculture
countries are so processed, packed, classified, packaged, transported and inspected, that there can he no doubt regarding their quantity and quality when they reach the market. In other words, he has to see to the quality and acceptability of the commodities that are exported.
That, in general terms, is the division which was laid out at that time as being the actual position as relating to the Department of Agriculture. And then he went on to say this with regard to the Department of Trade and Commerce-
But that commenced in 1936.
Well, it was in existence long before 1936; but I shall go into that matter later.
No.

The actual fact is that it did exist right back through the time the Hon. W. R. Motherwell was minister of agriculture in the government of Canada. That goes back to 1921. Then there was some question of whether it existed or not during the period of five years when Mr. Bennett was at the head of the government. But it was only a matter of discussion; it was not something which had actually been acted upon. Then, when we came in, just five years after we had gone out, this was the policy which was accepted and announced in 1938, as I have indicated here.
Then Mr. King went on to say:
"Acceptability" in this sense, that the effort cf the Minister of Agriculture is to ascertain the particular form and the quality and the kind of commodities most desired in the markets of the world. The jurisdiction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce begins with the matters of trade and of sale. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has to do with the business of sales, the business of trade in foreign countries. There need not necessarily be a conflict between the two. The line of margin where possible differences may arise, or at least have arisen in the past-they need not in the future if proper safeguards are observed-is with respect to the borderline I have described, where the Minister of Agriculture sees to it that products reach the old country and are there in a form for marketing that will be acceptable, and the part which the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his officials play in seeking to advertise these goods and to gain for them the widest possible sale.
That is the description of the activities of the two departments, and they have been carried on on that basis ever since. About the same time-I think it was 1936, when I took over the department-I had the estimates prepared in a manner different from what they had been prepared before. The estimates had been prepared by setting up each of the different divisions in the department upon commodities: that is, the dairy division was put by itself, the livestock division by itself, and so on, and each was

listed as one item. Speaking from memory I think there were fourteen items in the estimates at that time. There are some people who advocate following that policy today, namely the policy of getting back to fewer items in the estimates. That is being discussed in places other than the House of Commons. It is a matter of judgment of course as to whether the matter can be determined successfully in committees, or whether it can even be successfully discussed there.
In any case, in 1936 we re-organized the Department of Agriculture and put it under these divisions: administration service; science service; experimental farms service; production service and marketing service. Those were the five divisions of the department, and those divisions have been maintained ever since. Under each division appears a number of items, and those headings are presumed to set out for members of the House of Commons the items under which they can get information and discuss what is really going on in the different branches of the department.
Largely as a result of our experience as , we have gone along-some experiences gained during the war, and some from other sources-there have been added what we call specials. We started in with a few specials, but now the number has grown out of the general activities. The first one has to do with assistance in connection with cheese and cheese factories. We brought in an act which said that we should pay premiums on cheese under certain circumstances, and there was a special vote set up for it.
Then, we have another to provide assistance in the replacement of maple production equipment. There was a special act for that, and a special vote for it. It was exported that this last mentioned one would operate for only three or four years. However, the war came along, and it is still operating; and all payments have not yet been made under it.
The next one was the Agricultural Products Act, which was the act under which we made the agreements with Great Britain. We are still functioning in two or three of those. That is a special vote which was put in because we did not expect it would continue for all time as part of the activities of the department. When it did go out it would not interfere with the general divisions which are indicated here.
Then, item 38 in the estimates makes provision for assistance in the construction of potato warehouses under regulations to be approved by the governor in council.
How many have been constructed?

My hon. friend knows that better than I do. I think there have been three constructed in Prince Edward Island, one that is being discussed in Ontario and another discussed in Saskatchewan. I am not sure that there is any discussion at the present time in New Brunswick.

Yes, three on the island. At least three are on the island. My officials think there are six, but I know that there are three at least.

They are constructed; we are trying to agree on the method of paying for them. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, major irrigation and water conservation projects, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act; those are the activities and others are being carried on under the votes we are asking the house to pass. I think that is a hurried but rather complete outline of organization in this department.

While I am on my feet I want to say a word about the earlier statement of the minister as to the division of authority between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce in regard to the marketing of agricultural products. Last year we passed the Agricultural Products Marketing Act, which in effect gives to boards set up under provincial marketing legislation the power in interprovincial and export trade that those boards have in the marketing of those particular agricultural products within the province. Immediately those boards start to export, however, they will come under the regulations of the Department of Trade and Commerce, which may be quite different from those of the Department of Agriculture. It seems to me that we are going to run into difficulties in the marketing of agricultural products in that the regulations set up by the Department of Agriculture concerning marketing in Canada may not be the same as those of the Department of Trade and Commerce with respect to export trade. I wonder if the minister would comment on that?

Under the natural products marketing act of Saskatchewan, which is similar to the legislation in British Columbia and elsewhere, they have authority to set up a board and to say that all of that product delivered to the market must be delivered to the order of that board. When the board gets the product it is in exactly the same position as the Ford Motor Company or anyone else. They have the product, and they want to sell it. The Department of Trade and Commerce does not make regulations telling them how they are going to sell it. The Department of Trade and Commerce simply does for them what they do for everybody else. They try to find a market for that particular product, and inform them that it can be sold in a certain market at a certain price.
In so far as the Department of Agriculture is concerned we have said, under the act that was passed in 1949, that we will see that any board which is marketing farm products outside the province has the same rights and opportunity to do so, and all the safeguards, that are present in connection

Supply-Agriculture
with interprovincial marketing or international marketing. They will not be denied any of those things, so long as they do not overstep the provisions of the provincial law. We have undertaken to do that, but that does not interfere with the marketing of goods outside.

I was speaking particularly of the Department of Trade and Commerce, which sets up the grades for wheat that goes into the export trade. There are certain regulations and certain standards for the marketing of pork or dairy products within Canada. Conceivably the Department of Trade and Commerce could set different standards for the marketing of those products outside Canada, so there might easily be a conflict between the grades to be marketed within Canada and those to be marketed outside Canada.

No; the Department of Trade and Commerce has no grading system for any farm product except grain, and that is handled under the Canada Grain Act. All the other farm products are graded under systems set up with the Department of Agriculture, co-operating with the provincial departments. For example we had a grading system for butter in Alberta and Saskatchewan long before there was a grading system set up on the same basis in Ontario. We had different regulations governing trading between Manitoba and some of the other provinces for a considerable time. Eventually we succeeded in getting all provinces to cooperate with the federal government in having those different products graded according to the same standards. Where it is required that our officials do the grading for a province, the province appoints our man as their grader, and he does the grading for them. Where we require a provincial man to do the grading, we appoint him as our grader, and he does the job for us. The grades are the same right through the picture.
As I said a moment ago, we have six cargo men over in Britain. When a cargo comes in they take samples of the products that are sent over to see whether or not the grades have been maintained, but the remainder of the work in connection with it is done by the Department of Trade and Commerce.

I should like to point out to the minister that the potato growers of the maritime provinces have been disregarded in regard to the prices support act which was put into effect in 1944. At that time the minister stated the act would apply to all agricultural products except wheat, and would prevent them from going below the cost of production. In 1946 a program was put

into effect in New Brunswick which bolstered the price, and in 1948 the growers of potatoes were given support in the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. During the crop year of 1949-50 potatoes have been selling most of the time, at any rate since the first of the year, below the cost of production. The minister and the chairman of the agricultural prices support board have disregarded any request for relief under this support act.
Not more than two weeks ago the minister of agriculture in the province of New Brunswick telephoned the deputy minister of agriculture in Ottawa, and suggested that some support program be put into effect covering potatoes. It was felt it would only cost the department about $100,000 to stabilize the price of potatoes and to bring them up above the cost of production. This request was turned down. I wrote to Dr. A. M. Shaw, chairman of the agricultural prices support board, on May 5 as follows:
I wish to call your board's attention to the fact that potatoes are now selling way below cost of production and it does not seem that your board is paying any attention to the terms of the Agricultural Prices Support Act of 1944, which was put into effect to keep the price of agricultural products above cost of production, and I wish to point out that your board has disregarded the greatest agricultural food product grown which is the potato.
I further wish to point out that with an expenditure of $100,000 by your board, you could stabilize the price of potatoes on the Canadian market overnight. All you would have to do is put into effect a starch program for the balance of the season and the three factories, two in New Brunswick and one in Prince Edward Island, could not possibly use more than 100,000 barrels, and if you would guarantee the subsidy of $1 per barrel over the price that is being paid for starch potatoes in these two provinces it would have the effect of stabilizing the market throughout Canada for the balance of the season.
This action would have to be taken quickly and, with three inspectors, the factories I believe would co-operate with you under this scheme. You could buy the potatoes trader the same plan as you used for the 1946-47 crop; therefore, with little cost, your board could be a great aid to 3,000 or 4,000 cars of potatoes now left in the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
I also wrote to the minister on May 6, but I never received a reply from him. Dr. Shaw did reply to my letter on May 9, and here is what he says in the third paragraph of the letter:
As you know, it is not unusual, except in years of short supply, for the potato growers to have some wastage at the end of the season.
He intends to say that it is not unusual for potatoes to be dumped at the end of the season. The Agricultural Prices Support Act went through parliament in 1944. At the time the minister was piloting the act through the house, he said that no agricultural products would be dumped as long as he was

Minister of Agriculture. I say to him that potatoes were dumped last year, and potatoes will be dumped in the maritime provinces this year unless some support is given to the price. The idea of the chairman of the agricultural prices support board saying that we always dump potatoes in surplus years, when we have an act which the minister said was to stop the price of agricultural products falling below the cost of production! He was referring to all agricultural products, except wheat, and that includes potatoes.
On page 5622 of Hansard for July 29, 1944, we find that when the act was going through the house I asked the minister about this, and he said:
It is intended to cover all agricultural products, except wheat.

Yes, including corn. "Agricultural products" means any product of agriculture, except wheat, designated by the governor in council, and includes processed meat, dairy and poultry products if so designated.
He stated, on a dozen different occasions when asked, that that included all agricultural products. Potatoes were the first agricultural product that he helped under this act in 1946. Although they have been selling in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island for three or four months now below the cost of production, not a thing has been done by the department, although the department of agriculture in Prince Edward Island and the department of agriculture in New Brunswick have requested that something be done by the agricultural prices support board. I would hope that it is not too late for them still to try to stabilize the market for the rest of the season. Otherwise in my opinion, two or three thousand cars of potatoes are going to be dumped. What we are concerned about is that the time may come when the board may force the farmer to take less than the cost of production.

I would hope that that time will
not come and I do not think it is likely to under this bill.
I request now that the Minister of Agriculture take some immediate action to help
