I wish to say something more about the Department of Agriculture. It is about the experimental farm. When I came to parliament in 1940 the estimates for the central experimental farm amounted to $400,000; that is for the central experimental farm. Today the estimates before us amount to $1,800,000. I was out there to look around. All I saw was a lot of pegs driven into the ground. I do not know how they spend $1,800,000, or $1,400,000 more than they spent ten years ago. They have only about 300 acres more land than they had in 1940. What in the world they are doing with the money, I do not know. They are even buying a separate threshing machine now for every plot of grain they have growing out there so that they thresh it separately.
It is amusing to go out there and look around that farm. What the farmers get from it, I do not know. We in the maritime provinces do not get any help from it. We get some help from our provincial farms or rather from the federal farms located in the provinces; that is, the branch farms. We get some help from them, but we do not get any help from this central experimental farm. It is a nice place out there. It is a nice park and flower garden for Ottawa; but I do not think the farmers get much good from it. I think the provincial farms owned by the federal government are of some good; they are located in the different zones in the different provinces, carrying on research work in different things grown in these provinces.

I should like to ask the minister this question. It was reported in the fall of 1944 that he asked the provinces to take over the support of agricultural products in different sections of Canada. I believe in that move. I should like to ask him to answer whether he did consult the provinces. I understand that he did. The provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island turned him down. I think they made a great mistake in turning him down. I should like to know whether that is correct or not. I hope that at this late hour he will take some interest in the potato growers in the maritime provinces. The potato industry in the maritime provinces is practically the only industry the farmer has as a cash crop. It means everything to him. When the tariff is revised between the United States and Canada, I hope we get some reduction of duty. We pay 75 cents a hundred going into the United States. They pay nothing coming into Canada except from- June 15 to July 31. I think the duty in the United States should be lowered. I think we should have an ad valorem duty on potatoes. I cannot understand why two men would sit down across the table on tariffs and one would say, "You can go into our country with a certain commodity free"; and the United States representative says, "We are going to tax you 75 cents a hundred." It does not make common sense to me. I do not know why you would make an arrangement like that.

I wish to answer one or two direct questions. The last one that I was asked was as to whether at some time-I think in 1944 or around that time-I had suggested to the provinces that they should take over the marketing of potatoes, I suppose among other products. The facts are, in addition to that, that in 1938-which goes back further than 1944-the farm federation came to Ottawa and called to our attention the type of legislation in force in British Columbia. It was known as the natural products marketing act. It provided for the setting up of boards to market the products of that province, and particularly farm products. Prior to that they had taken the legislation to the privy council and had it declared intra vires. In their discussions they had concluded that they knew a kind of legislation which would be intra vires if it were passed here in order to supplement the proposal. We said at that time that we did not think that one province having acted was sufficient to warrant the dominion government passing complementary legislation.
The federation went back to the other provinces and asked them to pass similar legislation. My memory is that they succeeded in getting about six provinces to pass similar legislation within a year, or

a year and a half's time. If that is what my hon. friend means by asking, did I suggest at any time that the provinces ought to do this, then I say we suggested, when they came and told us that one province had already done so, that if they desired the federal government to bring in complementary legislation there should be considerably more than one province acting upon it before they came and asked us to do it. As I say, when they did come back the next time they had five or six provinces that had passed the legislation. But it happened to be within a few weeks after the war had started in 1939, and we said to them that we were going to set up government boards to handle the products during the war. We told them that we were going to operate them under the War Measures Act, and therefore we expected that so long as we had a War Measures Act, or some legislation which succeeded it, any boards which did operate would be federal government boards. The farm organization accepted that position and said they agreed that under the circumstances that is what ought to be done and that is what was done, and so we handled the different products. The dairy products boards handled the dairy products; the meat board handled the meat products; and we had a special products board which handled the other products. Those boards operated right through the period of the war, and down to a period after the war; in fact some of them are operating yet.
The federation did not come back until the war was over. In 1946 they did come back and they asked the federal government to pass this complementary legislation. We said that we were still operating under our own boards; and we refused to bring the legislation before the house in spite of the fact that the opposition was urging us to do so from time to time until 1949. In 1949 we brought the legislation before the house. That legislation provided that we would assist the boards that had been set up provincially by making it possible for them to apply outside the province the same principles as they were applying inside. That legislation is now on the statute books; and to the extent that I suggested that, it can be said that I more or less promoted the idea. But I must say that at no time did the government here during that period advocate that this ought to be done. We simply said that if the federation went out and succeeded in getting a considerable number of the provinces to fake that action we would consider the matter. We did consider it, brought it here, and it was passed.
I was asking about the support act.
The support act itself which came up in 1944 has nothing whatsoever to do with that matter.
Did you not ask the provinces to take over the support act; and did you not say that you would furnish the money if they would administer it?
No, I did not go that far. If my hon. friend will listen I will give him the whole story.
I think you did.
The position is, my hon. friend came to my office and advocated that, as he said a moment ago but I did not.
You advocated it.

I did not say that to the
provinces. The position taken in 1944-and I think my hon. friend will find the wording that I used is correct-is this. We did bring down legislation in 1944 which we intimated would probably be required to deal with staple products as we were getting out from under the organizations that had been set up under these boards, and the agreements that had been entered into by them, and that it would probably be necessary for us to stabilize prices over a period, and stabilize them at a level which would maintain the relationship between the farmers generally and those who were supplying them with commodities, to maintain a price level as between them which would be as satisfactory as the conditions had been in the last few years of the war.
Above cost of production.
You made your speech; let me make mine.
You said that in your speech in 1944.

In 1944 the position taken
was as I stated. If my hon. friend will go back and get the 1944 Hansard he will find that the one product we left doubt about was potatoes.
No.

We will get at that some
other time when we are on the item that has to do with potatoes. The position taken at that time-and I made it very clear to the house-was that if you put a floor price under potatoes which was as high as we were being asked to put under them by the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island we would have so many potatoes produced in this country that we would be in the position in 55946-171
Supply-Agriculture
which the Americans finally got by doing a similar thing. The position in regard to the sale of potatoes would then be very difficult particularly in view of the fact that two of the provinces of Canada depend absolutely upon the selling of potatoes, or a very considerable number of the farmers depend absolutely upon the sale of their potatoes in order to live at all. We in other parts of Canada are living fairly well without selling potatoes, particularly outside Canada.
I said it would be a mistake for us to set a price level for potatoes which would induce people right across Canada to produce potatoes. If we did that then we would be in trouble.
You did not say that in 1944.

That is the position that has been taken consistently all the way through from 1944 until now.
In marketing the 1948 crop we got into the position in February, I believe, of 1949, where we were being approached almost daily by those who were interested in the marketing of potatoes from New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Finally the agricultural prices support board entered into an arrangement whereby they would agree that any potatoes which were graded and in bins on a certain date would be taken over by the federal government at a certain price, I believe $1.15.
After the United States asked you to put on embargoes.

There are a lot of things
that I cannot take up in the few minutes I have left. That story can be told pretty well when we come to the item itself in the estimates. But we said at that time that we would take them over. We finally did get just approximately what my friend says they may have to dump this year, and we paid $1,600,000 for them. That is a pretty high price to pay for what was obtained, and even for the results that were obtained.
Coming to this year, a little before January we were asked to do the same thing again. At that time I said to them that we thought they should go ahead and market their potatoes. We thought that if we took any such action as has been suggested again we would be in difficulties with the United States, which today finds. itself with such an enormous supply of potatoes on hand that it is offering them at a cent a bag, and with that condition existing we could not afford to jeopardize the United States market for Canadian potatoes. And I must say that the Americans were buying potatoes, and are still buying potatoes. They were buying potatoes in

Supply-Agriculture
greater quantities than they bought them last year. We said we were not going to take a chance on spoiling any market we had in the United States by starting to subsidize potatoes on this side of the line in order to make it possible for people to ship them into the United States.
They do subsidize.

We have carried on under that plan up to the present time. We never have yet said to the people of New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island that we will not do anything whatsoever in order to assist them with the marketing of their potato crop this year. We never have said that at any time up to now. We have however kept ourselves in a position where we can take that position if we find it advisable to do so.
Now, what is the present position with regard to potatoes? In 1948, we marketed 17,159 cars. From the 1949 crop we marketed 22,885 cars, or we have marketed more than 5,000 more cars this year than last year.
You embargoed them last year?

Yes, I know, and we did not embargo them this year, and this year we sold them. Potatoes were sold into the market in the United States, and they are still being sold. As my hon. friend says, there might be some potatoes left over at the end of the season. No one knows that there are going to be. We have said, "Go ahead and sell them."
In so far as the stabilization of prices is concerned, on January 3, they had the highest price of this year, which was $1.35 basis Montreal.
You hope-

Now, you can read this all tomorrow and you will understand it better than if you try to talk at the same time as I am talking. On January 3 was the highest price of $1.35. The lowest price that has been obtained was $1.15 on February 7. And that happens to be exactly the price that we paid for 100 pounds of the surplus last year at the farm. We paid $1.15 last year for 100 pounds and the price has not been lower than $1.15 on the Montreal market for 75 pounds this year.
This year?
Yes, for a 75-pound bag this year.
Your support price was $1.15. That is what you are talking about?
I am not talking about that.
I know, but your support price last year-

The price on May 10 was $1.20 to $1.25. The highest price was $1.35, and the lowest, $1.15. I can hardly conceive of a product such as potatoes being more completely stabilized than apparently this product has been during that period of time. Whether it has been stabilized high enough might be another question. That is a question which can still be considered. No one has said here that we will not consider it.
But my learned friend makes the proposal that we should help out his starch company, and by doing what?
No, no.
By having these potatoes delivered at half the price which is being obtained for them on the market.
No, no.

Well, that is the suggestion, that we pay dollar for dollar, and put the potatoes into the starch plant. It would not all be in my hon. friend's starch plant, but it would be in somebody's starch plant.

On a point of privilege, the suggestion was made by the provincial government of New Brunswick that we pay 50 cents a barrel and the federal government pay a subsidy of one dollar a barrel. Fifty cents a barrel for starch potatoes today would not give the starch manufacturer one cent.
Mr. , Gardiner: Well, that is even worse than I thought it was. We are going to be asked to pay $2 for every one they pay. But in any case the suggestion is that we get rid of these extra 2,000 cars by putting them through starch plants, and that we subsidize the putting of them through the starch plants.
No.
Well, that is the way I understand it; and I do not know how you can make starch from potatoes without putting them through a starch plant.
It was only the effect of having them on the market.

In any case, that is the position in regard to potatoes. We have sold 5,000 more cars of potatoes-at least, they. have been sold; I should not say we sold them, because I would imagine my hon. friend sold as many as anybody else. There are five or six exporters of potatoes in New Brunswick, and they are very successful agents in marketing their product.
The only thing I have suggested is that a probable solution for their problem down there is for those five or six men to have

themselves appointed a board by the provincial government, and then starting in and marketing those potatoes in the interests of all the producers, rather than just in the interest of the agent who happens to be marketing them. If any suggestion has been made, then it has been that one. As a matter of fact that is the plan that was followed in Ontario under my hon. friend's leader, while he was premier of that province, in connection with the marketing of beans.
There are 200 licensed shippers in New Brunswick.

But those 200 licensed shippers do just as a lot of shippers do elsewhere- they operate through a few exporters. Those exporters have done a very successful business down in that part of the country. As a result of doing that successful business they have very large plants to put the potatoes through.
I think that in connection with all these matters we should do just what we did last year in winding up our activities in connection with apples. The apple growers came to us at the beginning of the season and they said, "We want you to make an agreement with us, just the same as you did during the war. We want an agreement whereby you will guarantee a return through assisting us to export or put them in cans, dehydrate them, and eventually wind up the season so that we will have a certain amount of return for our producers."
Well, eventually we said to them that we thought the time had come when, so far as possible, we should get out of those transactions. The apple growers are very well organized in at least two areas, namely, Nova Scotia and British Columbia, and they market their apples through their own organization. We said, "Go ahead and see what kind of job you can do of it." Well, the British Columbia board marketed apples in thirty-two states in the .United States, in spite of the fact that the Americans had one of the biggest apple crops they had ever grown. The British Columbia people went to the United States and merchandised their apples over there. They had them packed properly before they were shipped. Their apples were put on the market right alongside American apples, and under those conditions they sold in thirty-two states of the union.
Then, having done that, they found they could not sell all of their apples of certain varieties, and they gave those apples to Great Britain. My understanding is that the British government, in turn, did not sell them, but that they distributed at least a large part, if not all of them, to school children. That is they had been received as gifts, and those 55946-1711
Supply-Agriculture
apples were distributed more or less by way of gifts to the children in Great Britain. In any case the British Columbia people did not get any return from them. I believe it cost them about twenty-five cents to have them packed and placed on the ships; and the British paid the freight across the ocean.
Those apples were delivered in Great Britain. I might say that Nova Scotia marketed its apples just about as well as they have ever been marketed. Then, after they got through with those transactions, they came back and said, "This is our position." We checked the position with other apple producers in Canada, and did give a final payment to them indicating to them that from now on we expected them to go on and market their own product from year to year.
There was a by-election.

There was not any by-election at the time. That was done when there was no by-election in sight. I cannot understand my hon. friend knowing the effect that could have if that were to go down to the constituency where his own candidate is running. He is the solicitor for this organization and sat in this house for a short time. When I put the question to him across the floor of the house whether there was any politics in connection with the handling of apples in the Annapolis valley, as every hon. member who was in the house then knows, his answer was that there had not been. If the story goes down from the opposition in this house that there was politics in the handling of apples in the Annapolis valley during the ten-year period in which assistance has been given from Ottawa I venture to say it will get us more votes than anything else we could do. I suggest to my hon. friend that he go right on doing that if he wishes to help us politically.
The people in the Annapolis valley know what assistance they got. They know why they got it. They know how they got it. They got all the assistance they did through their own organization. When the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre chips in I would remind him that he is becoming more and more a Tory every day. Every time someone in the official opposition wants to interfere with anything that is being said over here the hon. member gives them a little help and boosts them along.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Maybe they need it.
I would like to suggest to the hon. member that the board they have in Nova Scotia-

What are you doing for Nova Scotia potatoes?

Supply-Agriculture

The position in Nova Scotia as well as in British Columbia is that they have commodity boards of the type that has always been advocated by my hon. friend's party. I challenge him to say that they have not. Their party has always advocated commodity boards. They have always said, that boards such as they have in British Columbia are the kind of organization that should be set up to market farm products. There is one of those boards in Nova Scotia marketing farm products. That board was organized by the growers and it is operated by the growers and they sell their apples in the interests of the producers. They are not playing politics with anyone.

The minister has been quoting figures that have been paid for potatoes. I happen to have on my desk a letter dated May 2 from a young veteran who went into the potato business at the close of the war. This man tells me that the price to the producer today, that would be on May 2, for No. 1 table stock was 40 cents per bushel and 67 cents per 100 pound sack.
Where?

That is at a place called O'Leary Station in Prince Edward Island. He goes on to state that the floor price last year was 69 cents per bushel and $1.14 per 100 pound sack. The minister gave the price for a 75 pound bag, which would be at Montreal. That would mean that this young man would get 51 cents for a 75 pound sack. I agree with the minister that probably the solution is a commodity board, but these young fellows have invested their war savings in potato growing and they have their cellars full of potatoes and the prices are ruinous as far as they are concerned. I shall not go into the other .side of the matter but I do intend to raise something else when the proper item is before us.

We have got away from
potatoes, but only to say that what can be done in the case of apples can be done in the case of potatoes. No one can say at this moment that the door is closed in connection with the handling of potatoes. We are going to deal with potatoes at the end of the picture when we know what the situation is and what has been done. The hon. .member has just raised the question of potatoes selling at a certain price. You have to consider the average price to the grower. You cannot talk about what happens at the end of the season when you . are always dumping some potatoes as though the price received represented the return.
They were not able to sell them before.

They say that, but people who have been talking to me say that there has been proper distribution. The records show that to the producers from August to January in 1948-49 the average price for potatoes was 99 cents per 100 pounds. In the same period in 1949-50 the average price was 98 cents per 100 pounds. In other words, there has been a difference of only one cent in the two seasons. We did give some support in the one season, while in the other season we have not given any support. The farmers were paid more money for their potatoes partly because they had more to sell.
Not the small grower.
We can discuss that at some other time.
The large grower who is also a dealer can sell his potatoes first.

That brings us back to what my hon. friend mentioned a moment ago. Every time these potato growers have come asking for assistance I have told them that it can best be done by means of an organization in their own area. After the point is reached where the producer does not get the average price, where he gets only the minimum price, it is not fair to say that is the price. We are absolutely opposed to that kind of policy being followed. The average price for the year has been 98 cents, and it was 99 cents last year.
Where is that?

That is the price to the grower, as I said at the beginning of my remarks. If my hon. friend had been listening he would have known that. I am sorry if the hon. member in front of him was talking so much that I can understand my hon. friend not hearing me.
Would that be at the farm?

To the grower at the farm. That is the price the grower got for his potatoes. I suppose he would deliver them at the village or in town or probably at the railroad station, but in any case that is his price.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
